findings.title: Feature-consistency pruning can delete the uniquely optimal initial action despite exact vector-value representation
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-252__I01 — Feature-consistency pruning can delete the uniquely optimal initial action despite exact vector-value representation
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages 1–3, especially the second contribution on page 3; Section 5.3, pages 10–14, Definition 3 and equations (7)–(10); Algorithm 1 and the initial-action construction on page 15. The admissible scalarizations are defined on page 5.

**Claim.** The method covers coordinatewise nondecreasing scalarization functions, including nonlinear preferences. Its advertised completeness contribution is that all scalarization-optimal policies can be found while considering only polynomially many future policies. The proposed computational reduction retains only future policies that maximize a scalar linear function of the chosen features. That reduction is not justified by exact linear representation of each component of the vector Q-function.

**Error and evidence.** A two-stage, two-objective MOMDP gives a counterexample where every learned vector Q-function is exact and the published pruning removes the only optimal initial action.

There is one initial state with four actions H, C1, C2 and C3. At the terminal stage there are four states, ordered (-1,0,1,z), with two actions A and B. For real-valued states x in {-1,0,1}, rewards are

\[
R_2(x,A)=(2+x,2-x), \qquad R_2(x,B)=(3/2,3/2).
\]

At z, rewards are R2(z,A)=(0,0) and R2(z,B)=(-1,-1). Initial action H has immediate reward zero and transitions to (-1,0,1) with probabilities (9/10,1/20,1/20). Each C action transitions deterministically to z and has the following immediate reward:

| Action | Immediate reward |
|---|---|
| C1 | (1.16, 2.86) |
| C2 | (1.085, 2.885) |
| C3 | (1.61, 1.51) |

Use the terminal feature map

\[
\phi_2(s,a)=(1,x,1_{\{a=A\}},x1_{\{a=A\}},1_{\{s=z\}},1_{\{s=z\}}1_{\{a=A\}}),
\]

where x(z)=0. Both terminal reward coordinates are represented exactly. Their coefficient columns are respectively

\[
(3/2,0,1/2,1,-5/2,1/2)^\top,\qquad
(3/2,0,1/2,-1,-5/2,1/2)^\top .
\]

Use one-hot initial-action features. Thus all vector Q-values at both stages lie exactly in their stated regression spaces.

The terminal Pareto NDP allows both actions at -1 and 1, and only A at 0 and z. Its four consistent deterministic policies have these H returns; the policy names below omit the final, always-A choice at z:

| Terminal policy at (-1,0,1) | Exact expected H return | Retained by the published feature-consistency constraints? |
|---|---|---|
| A-A-A | (1.15, 2.85) | Yes |
| A-A-B | (1.075, 2.875) | Yes |
| B-A-A | (1.6, 1.5) | Yes |
| B-A-B | (1.525, 1.525) | **No** |

For any scalar linear feature score, the A-minus-B score at the real states is c+dx. The strict-margin constraints in equation (9) require, for B-A-B,

\[
c-d\leq-1,\qquad c\geq1,\qquad c+d\leq-1.
\]

Adding the two endpoint inequalities gives c≤-1, contradicting c≥1. The z features cannot change these three inequalities. This is an exact infeasibility certificate, not a numerical or tie-breaking failure.

Now use the permitted, strictly coordinatewise increasing preference

\[
\rho(v)=\min(v_1,v_2)+(v_1+v_2)/100.
\]

H followed by B-A-B has utility 3111/2000=1.5555. It is the unique best H continuation on reachable states and is better than every C action; the best alternative is C3, with utility 3853/2500=1.5412. Policies using B at the center or at z cannot improve these values because A strictly dominates B there. At each real terminal state, B-A-B is also the unique local maximizer of this same preference. The example therefore does not rely on preference changes or a conflict between local and initial choices.

After feature pruning, each remaining H return is strictly dominated by another initial action: C1 dominates (1.15,2.85), C2 dominates (1.075,2.875), and C3 dominates (1.6,1.5). Consequently, the page-14/page-15 existential NDP construction **deletes H**. With all four terminal consistent policies, H is retained. With the published three-policy collection, the recommended initial set is {C1,C2,C3}; following those recommendations incurs utility loss at least 143/10000=0.0143.

The same calculation is a literal finite-data fitted-Q counterexample. Take 160 trajectories: 40 beginning with H, with terminal-state counts 36,2,2 and equal A/B observations at each state, and 40 beginning with each C action, all reaching z, again equally split between terminal actions. The terminal design matrix has rank 6; its least-squares fit is the exact displayed reward function. The initial one-hot design has rank 4. For each of all 16 possible terminal maps, equation (4) yields exactly the true corresponding initial expected return. Thus neither sampling error, an unobserved action, misspecified vector Q-functions, nor numerical regression error explains the deletion.

Reproduction uses exact rational arithmetic for rewards, returns, normal-equation fits and utility comparisons, plus a separate feasibility LP for each policy. See the control results and the executable check. Independently derived rational design/backups and the same deletion are recorded in bounded independent QA.

**Reason for rejection.** Computing all nonlinear-preference-optimal choices with the proposed polynomial future-policy collection is a named central contribution. The counterexample invalidates that combination of completeness and pruning even with exact fitted vector values, and causes a genuinely optimal initial treatment/action to be excluded from the delivered decision support. The scalar fitted-Q analogy on pages 12–13 does not establish the needed inference: applying a nonlinear preference to a linear vector Q-function need not yield a policy representable as the argmax of any scalar linear feature score.

One can explicitly restrict the allowable preference-induced policies to the feature-consistent class, or enrich the features to fix this particular example. Neither supplies the advertised completeness for arbitrary permitted preferences at the chosen feature dimension. Enumerating all NDP-consistent policies avoids this pruning loss but gives up the stated polynomial reduction. A new completeness-preserving policy representation or a materially narrower contribution is required. Theorem 1's polynomial upper bound for the restricted policy class remains intact; the finding does not establish erroneous CATIE counts or clinical outcomes.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the move from vector Q-regression to polynomial policy enumeration, the scalar-linear greedy-policy restriction appeared incompatible with nonlinear scalarization.

**Verification method.** Read the full paper and rechecked the rendered definitions, constraints, algorithm and central contribution statements. Constructed the exact terminal policy obstruction, then added competing initial actions to verify actual deletion from the delivered NDP. Enumerated all terminal maps, solved their margin feasibility problems, and verified every backup with full-rank exact rational regression. A separate reviewer independently checked the original scope and reproduced the strengthened 160-trajectory certificate.

**Confidence.** **High.** The infeasible inequalities and finite rational computations directly demonstrate the failed completeness claim and the excluded optimal initial action. The finding concerns the published algorithm and does not depend on unavailable historical experimental code or data.

findings.title: The proposed global solver can optimize outside the required rank constraint
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-273__I01 — The proposed global solver can optimize outside the required rank constraint
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page12, paragraph immediately after Remark1 (the prescribed factor width k=r+1); page13, Equations29–32 and the claim that convergence is guaranteed for the rank-constrained problem30. The global-solver contribution is also asserted in the abstract, PDF page1; the introduction, page4; and the first paragraph of page8. The underlying estimator is P1/Equation8, page7, and its statistical theorem is Theorem1, pages8–9.

**Claim.** P1 estimates a matrix with rank at most r and entrywise magnitude at most alpha. The paper factors X=UVᵀ, states that choosing k=r+1 columns suffices for global convergence when r bounds the rank of the true matrix, and proposes a gradient method for the rank-constrained barrier objective30. It invokes a certificate for a *rank-deficient local minimum of the factors* to justify this prescription. Its updates and output contain no projection or truncation back to rank r.

**Error and evidence.** The rank bound on the true matrix does not imply the needed rank deficiency of the optimizer of the empirical objective. The prescribed width permits matrices of rank r+1, including global factor optima that are infeasible for P1 and30.

Consider this complete instance under the paper's own model:

- m=n=2, r=1, alpha=1, and the true matrix M=0, which belongs to C.
- Observe every entry. The bi-adjacency matrix is all ones, with row degree2, top singular value2, uniform left/right top singular vectors, and second singular value0. Both A1 and A2 hold.
- Use binary logistic quantization with sigma=1 and boundary0. Both links are strictly log-concave, and gamma_alpha is positive on[-1,1].
- Let the observed labels be [[2,2],[2,1]], equivalently encoded by S=[[1,1],[1,-1]]. At true M=0 the independent observations realize this pattern with probability1/16.

For the allowed barrier parameter lambda=1, the matrix objective in29 is

    F_tilde(X) = sum_ij [log(1 + exp(-S_ij X_ij)) - log(1 - X_ij²)].

Define g(t)=log(1+exp(-t))-log(1-t²) for |t|<1. It has g''(t)≥2 and a unique minimizer t>0 satisfying

    -1/(1+exp(t)) + 2t/(1-t²) = 0.

An exact bracket is1/5<t<1/4: exp(1/5)<5/4 makes the derivative at1/5 negative, while exp(1/4)>1 makes it positive at1/4. Therefore the unique global matrix minimizer is

    X_star = t S,           det(X_star) = -2t² != 0.

Its rank is2. The prescribed k=r+1=2 factorization represents it, for example with U=I₂ and V=tS. The matrix gradient is zero there, so it is a stationary global minimum of the factorized problem. It is not a saddle point. Yet it violates the rank≤1 constraint in30 and P1.

This is a strict optimization mismatch. The two singular values of X_star are sqrt(2)t. Every rank-one matrix has squared Frobenius distance at least2t² from it. Since F_tilde is2-strongly convex, every feasible rank-one matrix has objective value at least

    F_tilde(X_star) + 2t² > F_tilde(X_star) + 2/25.

Thus the global factor optimum cannot also be a solution of30. The phenomenon holds for every lambda>0: replace the barrier by-lambda log(1-t²), giving a unique positive t_lambda and rank-two optimum t_lambda S. Taking a small penalty or following lambda toward0 does not restore rank feasibility. Without the barrier, the unique full-box likelihood optimum is S, also rank2. Repeating the rows and columns of S yields the same mismatch at arbitrarily large even dimensions.

For a numerical reproduction, the scalar root at lambda1 is .21327724396889633 and the rank-one barrier objective gap is at least .0909743655899. An independent implementation of the displayed factor-gradient updates with Armijo search, starting from balanced factors whose product is .1S, converges in41 iterations to tS; every recorded product has rank2. This is an independently implemented check of the equations, not a rerun of unpublished author code.

The paper's cited rank-deficiency principle does not fill the gap. [Bach, Mairal and Ponce, Proposition4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.1869v1) concerns a rank-deficient local factor minimum of a convex empirical objective. It does not derive that condition from the rank of the unknown data-generating matrix. In this example both factors at the global empirical optimum have full column rank.

**Reason for rejection.** A globally convergent method for the exact rank-constrained estimator is an explicit central contribution. The proposed formulation instead permits a strictly better but infeasible matrix, so the claimed solver guarantee fails even when optimization reaches a global factor minimum. The statistical recovery theorem is conditional on an actual global minimizer of the rank-r constrained likelihood; it does not establish the theorem's guarantee for this infeasible output. Setting k=r or truncating the output can enforce rank feasibility, but supplies no global rank-r optimization certificate. Relabeling the estimator as rank r+1 also does not make the rank of its empirical optimum follow from the true rank bound. Restoring the claimed contribution requires a valid constrained global algorithm/certificate or a materially different guarantee, rather than a constant correction or routine proof clarification. The conditional statistical theorem and historical experimental scores are not refuted by this finding.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the global-convergence argument, distinguished the rank of the true matrix from the rank of the empirical convex optimizer in the invoked factorization certificate.

**Verification method.** Read all34 pages, including both appendices, then rechecked the original rendered estimator, rank-width prescription and update equations. Derived the exact separable counterexample, proved all model/graph premises, strict rank infeasibility and positive objective gap, independently implemented an Armijo trajectory, and checked the cited proposition. A separate bounded audit of the original pages and70-digit root computations independently confirmed the counterexample for lambda1,.1,.001. No historical empirical failure is inferred.

**Confidence: High.** An exact finite instance satisfies the stated assumptions and gives a full-rank global factor optimum with a strictly positive gap to every permitted rank-one matrix. The conclusion does not depend on optimizer tolerances, saddle-point behavior or unavailable experimental artifacts.

The global-solver contribution is also asserted in the abstract, PDF page1; the introduction, page4; and the first paragraph of page8. The underlying estimator is P1/Equation8, page7, and its statistical theorem is Theorem1, pages8–9.

Claim. P1 estimates a matrix with rank at most r and entrywise magnitude at most alpha. The paper factors X=UVᵀ, states that choosing k=r+1 columns suffices for global convergence when r bounds the rank of the true matrix, and proposes a gradient method for the rank-constrained barrier objective30. It invokes a certificate for a rank-deficient local minimum of the factors to justify this prescription. Its updates and output contain no projection or truncation back to rank r.

Error and evidence. The rank bound on the true matrix does not imply the needed rank deficiency of the optimizer of the empirical objective. The prescribed width permits matrices of rank r+1, including global factor optima that are infeasible for P1 and30.

Consider this complete instance under the paper's own model:

  • m=n=2, r=1, alpha=1, and the true matrix M=0, which belongs to C.
  • Observe every entry. The bi-adjacency matrix is all ones, with row degree2, top singular value2, uniform left/right top singular vectors, and second singular value0. Both A1 and A2 hold.
  • Use binary logistic quantization with sigma=1 and boundary0. Both links are strictly log-concave, and gamma_alpha is positive on[-1,1].
  • Let the observed labels be [[2,2],[2,1]], equivalently encoded by S=[[1,1],[1,-1]]. At true M=0 the independent observations realize this pattern with probability1/16.

For the allowed barrier parameter lambda=1, the matrix objective in29 is

F_tilde(X) = sum_ij [log(1 + exp(-S_ij X_ij)) - log(1 - X_ij²)].

Define g(t)=log(1+exp(-t))-log(1-t²) for |t|<1. It has g''(t)≥2 and a unique minimizer t>0 satisfying

-1/(1+exp(t)) + 2t/(1-t²) = 0.

An exact bracket is1/5<t<1/4: exp(1/5)<5/4 makes the derivative at1/5 negative, while exp(1/4)>1 makes it positive at1/4. Therefore the unique global matrix minimizer is

X_star = t S,           det(X_star) = -2t² != 0.

Its rank is2. The prescribed k=r+1=2 factorization represents it, for example with U=I₂ and V=tS. The matrix gradient is zero there, so it is a stationary global minimum of the factorized problem. It is not a saddle point. Yet it violates the rank≤1 constraint in30 and P1.

This is a strict optimization mismatch. The two singular values of X_star are sqrt(2)t. Every rank-one matrix has squared Frobenius distance at least2t² from it. Since F_tilde is2-strongly convex, every feasible rank-one matrix has objective value at least

F_tilde(X_star) + 2t² > F_tilde(X_star) + 2/25.

Thus the global factor optimum cannot also be a solution of30. The phenomenon holds for every lambda>0: replace the barrier by-lambda log(1-t²), giving a unique positive t_lambda and rank-two optimum t_lambda S. Taking a small penalty or following lambda toward0 does not restore rank feasibility. Without the barrier, the unique full-box likelihood optimum is S, also rank2. Repeating the rows and columns of S yields the same mismatch at arbitrarily large even dimensions.

For a numerical reproduction, the scalar root at lambda1 is .21327724396889633 and the rank-one barrier objective gap is at least .0909743655899. An independent implementation of the displayed factor-gradient updates with Armijo search, starting from balanced factors whose product is .1S, converges in41 iterations to tS; every recorded product has rank2. This is an independently implemented check of the equations, not a rerun of unpublished author code.

The paper's cited rank-deficiency principle does not fill the gap. Bach, Mairal and Ponce, Proposition4 concerns a rank-deficient local factor minimum of a convex empirical objective. It does not derive that condition from the rank of the unknown data-generating matrix. In this example both factors at the global empirical optimum have full column rank.

Reason for rejection. A globally convergent method for the exact rank-constrained estimator is an explicit central contribution. The proposed formulation instead permits a strictly better but infeasible matrix, so the claimed solver guarantee fails even when optimization reaches a global factor minimum. The statistical recovery theorem is conditional on an actual global minimizer of the rank-r constrained likelihood; it does not establish the theorem's guarantee for this infeasible output. Setting k=r or truncating the output can enforce rank feasibility, but supplies no global rank-r optimization certificate. Relabeling the estimator as rank r+1 also does not make the rank of its empirical optimum follow from the true rank bound. Restoring the claimed contribution requires a valid constrained global algorithm/certificate or a materially different guarantee, rather than a constant correction or routine proof clarification. The conditional statistical theorem and historical experimental scores are not refuted by this finding.

Discovery method. While tracing the global-convergence argument, distinguished the rank of the true matrix from the rank of the empirical convex optimizer in the invoked factorization certificate.

Verification method. Read all34 pages, including both appendices, then rechecked the original rendered estimator, rank-width prescription and update equations. Derived the exact separable counterexample, proved all model/graph premises, strict rank infeasibility and positive objective gap, independently implemented an Armijo trajectory, and checked the cited proposition. A separate bounded audit of the original pages and70-digit root computations independently confirmed the counterexample for lambda1,.1,.001. No historical empirical failure is inferred.

Confidence: High. An exact finite instance satisfies the stated assumptions and gives a full-rank global factor optimum with a strictly positive gap to every permitted rank-one matrix. The conclusion does not depend on optimizer tolerances, saddle-point behavior or unavailable experimental artifacts.

findings.title: The dimension-independent projection accuracy bound fails, invalidating the fixed-accuracy justification for the second algorithm
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-319__I01 — The dimension-independent projection accuracy bound fails, invalidating the fixed-accuracy justification for the second algorithm
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section 3.4, PDF pages 18–20; Discussion, page 29; Appendix A.3, pages 36–38, especially the conjectured extremal form and bound t>0.7 on page 38. The affected algorithm is the quadratic moment/null-space projection in Algorithms 5 and 8, pages 19 and 34.

**Claim.** For four stable power sums at exponents P/4,P/2,3P/4,P, the quadratic projection's relative error is claimed to be below 1−0.7^(4/P), independently of vector length. Page 18 and Appendix A expressly identify the underlying extremal assertion as a conjecture. Page 20 nevertheless uses it to select a maximum exponent independent of length for a prescribed error, and thereby justifies the second algorithm's O(k log k) complexity at that accuracy. In particular, it states that P=512 suffices for 0.5% relative error on the top contour.

**Error and evidence.** The conjectured universal lower bound is false. Consider a vector v containing one entry 1, 1,000 entries 1/2, and 1,000 entries 1/4. Its first four power sums are exactly

\[
m_1=751,\quad m_2=627/2,\quad m_3=1133/8,\quad m_4=2157/32.
\]

Using the paper's own moment-polynomial formula gives

\[
\gamma_2=m_1m_3-m_2^2=64625/8,\qquad
\gamma_1=m_2m_3-m_1m_4=-199125/32,\qquad
\gamma_0=m_2m_4-m_3^2=34375/32.
\]

The maximum polynomial root—the quantity t after the change of variables on page 36—is therefore

\[
t=\frac{1593+\sqrt{262849}}{4136}
  \approx0.509112189142479 < 0.7.
\]

An exact inequality check avoids relying on decimal root evaluation: the upward-opening polynomial has its vertex at 1593/4136<7/10 and its value at 7/10 is 43305/64>0, so its larger root lies below 7/10. The discriminant and denominator are positive.

To make this a literal, numerically stable top-contour example with P=64, set

\[
u_i=(4/5)v_i^{1/16}.
\]

The four power sums of u at exponents 16,32,48,64 are (4/5)^(16j)m_j. Numerically, they are

\[
21.13877075,\quad 0.2483802895,\quad
0.003158343039,\quad 0.00004231158889.
\]

All exceed the stated FFT stability threshold 10^(-12), and both relevant moment determinants exceed the division guard 10^(-10). The true maximum is 0.8. Quadratic projection returns

\[
\widehat\alpha=(4/5)t^{1/16}\approx0.766947843136,
\]

with relative error approximately **4.13152%**, exceeding the asserted **2.20455%** bound.

The explicit 0.5% statement at P=512 also fails. Use u=(99/100)v^(1/128). All four required power sums remain stable. The true maximum is 0.99, while the exact relative error is 1−t^(1/128), approximately **0.526%**, above 0.5% and above the claimed 1−0.7^(1/128) bound. This is not an error caused by too few stable moments, a repeated-root degeneracy, or floating-point cancellation.

These vectors occur in actual max-convolution inputs satisfying the prescribed normalization. For the P=64 example, let L be a length-2002 vector of ones and let R be u followed by one final entry 1. Both inputs have maximum 1. At output index 2000, the products defining u^(2000) are exactly the entries of u, with the last R entry excluded.

The authenticated author implementation was recovered from the paper's Bitbucket repository at commit 6934174ad801e7bb6c494fdb3218d685a9ddfc04, dated November 4, 2015. Its history identifies the projection addition on October 22, 2015. Executing the original functions after Python 3 compatibility changes reproduces the 4.13152% projection error in this full convolution. With the optional affine correction enabled, this particular output is corrected, but index 0 changes from the correct value 0.8 to approximately 0.828364600709, a **3.54558%** relative error. Thus the optional correction does not restore the advertised bound for this input. The exact moment/root counterexample, independently of the native run, establishes that the underlying conjecture is false.

There is no replacement positive universal constant that repairs this argument. For

\[
v_N=(1,\underbrace{a,\ldots,a}_{N},
        \underbrace{b,\ldots,b}_{N}),\qquad 0<b<a<1,
\]

the jth power sum divided by N converges to a^j+b^j. Dividing the quadratic coefficients by N² gives the limiting polynomial

\[
ab(a-b)^2(x-a)(x-b).
\]

Its largest root is a. Choosing a arbitrarily small makes the limiting t arbitrarily small. The proposed worst-case form (1,a,b,b,...) misses distributions with two large groups of submaximum values. Hence the error's dependence on length cannot be removed from this projection by replacing 0.7 with another fixed positive number.

 The native results are fresh verification runs, not reproductions of the paper's historical random experiments.

**Reason for rejection.** The second named contribution promises a stronger accuracy/runtime trade-off than the first piecewise norm method. Its fixed-exponent, length-independent accuracy justification rests directly on the false conjecture, and the paper's concrete exponent/error prescription fails on ordinary finite normalized inputs. The issue is a demonstrated contradiction, not simply the absence of a proof for a conjecture. The arbitrarily small limiting roots rule out a routine numerical adjustment of the constant.

The projection still runs in O(k log k) with a fixed number of FFTs and can work well on the displayed examples. What fails is the stated accuracy justification for fixing that number independently of length. Recovering the advertised trade-off requires a new argument with substantively different assumptions or a changed algorithm/exponent schedule; restricting the conclusion to an empirical heuristic withdraws a central claimed advantage. This finding does not refute the basic FFT power-sum identity, the qualitative speed advantage, or the historical HMM plot.

**Discovery method.** Inspecting the Appendix A extremal-form conjecture suggested that one isolated maximum could be concealed by two large groups of smaller values, rather than by the proposed single repeated bulk value.

**Verification method.** Read the full paper and appendix and inspected the rendered equations, algorithm, assumptions and accuracy/runtime statements. Derived exact rational moments and the polynomial root, checked its inequality against 0.7, verified numerical stability and normalization, embedded it in a full convolution, and ran the authenticated author projection with and without affine correction. Checked the limiting family algebraically. Separate random norm/two-support controls and exact HMM controls were used to check the implementation and unaffected identities. A second reviewer independently reproduced the rational root, P=64/P=512 stable violations and limiting polynomial, and inspected original pages 18–20, 34 and 38; this was bounded verification, not a second full-paper review. See independent QA.

**Confidence.** **High.** The finite exact root refutes the claimed universal bound, the asymptotic family excludes a constant-only repair, and the author code reproduces the failure under stable numerical conditions. Historical economic data and random seeds are not needed for the finding.

findings.title: The proposed boundary-constrained variational problem generally has no solution, and the published finite-element solver is inconsistent
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-327__I01 — The proposed boundary-constrained variational problem generally has no solution, and the published finite-element solver is inconsistent
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages5–8, Section3, especially the admissible set and objective(7), the full-row equations(14), (17)–(18), and the convergence assertion at the end of page8; PDF pages9–10, the central local construction(19)–(21); PDF page27, AppendixB. The dependence of the proposed method on this construction is stated in the abstract/PDF1, introduction/PDF2–3, and conclusion/PDF26.

**Claim.** For a bounded Lipschitz domain, the paper constrains the prediction by requiring a vector-valued H1 function to have a prescribed prediction trace on the boundary. It proposes minimizing

\[
J(u)=\int_\Omega\{\tfrac12u^\top A u-f^\top u\}
\]

over that trace-constrained set. Here A is the positive definite local noisy GP covariance matrix and f is the vector of covariances with a test location. The paper then says to solve its finite-element linear system with the prescribed boundary coefficients, and asserts that the approximations converge to the original solution as the mesh tends to zero. This is the boundary-constrained solver on which patched GP is built.

**Error and evidence.** The objective contains no derivative term. Its coercivity is only in L2; it does not make the prescribed H1 trace stable under minimization. In general the proposed continuous problem has an unattained infimum, rather than the claimed boundary-constrained solution.

An exact example uses the admissible zero-mean constant GP covariance k(x,t)=1, observation noise variance1, one local observation at x=1/2 with y=1, and domain (0,1). Then A=2, f(x)=1, and a constant boundary prediction b=1/3 is a valid H1/2 trace. The feasible set is nonempty; for example u=1/3 is feasible. However,

\[
J(u)=\int_0^1(u(x)-\tfrac12)^2\,dx-\tfrac14.
\]

Let u equal1/2 on [epsilon,1−epsilon] and interpolate linearly to1/3 at both endpoints. This is an admissible H1 function and

\[
J(u)+\tfrac14=\epsilon/54\longrightarrow0.
\]

Thus the infimum is −1/4. Attaining it would require u=1/2 almost everywhere. Its H1 trace is1/2, contradicting the prescribed trace1/3. No minimizer exists. The squared derivative norm of this boundary-layer sequence is 1/(18 epsilon), so it does not converge in H1 to a trace-feasible limit.

The issue is not specific to a degenerate kernel or an arbitrary supplied boundary. Use the paper's own exponential covariance k(x,t)=exp(−|x−t|), noise variance1, local training pair(1/2,1), and neighboring pair(3/2,0). The unconstrained local coefficient is q(x)=exp(−|x−1/2|)/2. At their shared boundary x=1, the local prediction is exp(−1/2)/2. The paper's boundary GP rule(22), using these two observations, instead estimates

\[
b(1)=\frac{e^{-1/2}}{2+e^{-1}},
\]

which differs from q(1). Completing the square gives J(u)−J(q)=integral(u−q)^2. A boundary layer can again make this arbitrarily small, while equality is impossible under the different trace. Consequently a boundary value produced by the method itself creates the same nonexistence.

The published discrete equations fail separately in a finite, exact calculation. Take the constant-kernel example and conforming piecewise-linear basis at nodes0,1/2,1. Its mass matrix and right-hand side are

\[
\Phi=\frac1{12}
\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&4&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad FA^{-1}=\Phi
\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\1/2\\1/2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The first line of(17), or(20), retains all rows of the unconstrained equation Phi U=F A-inverse. Since Phi is invertible, it forces every nodal coefficient to1/2. The boundary equation(18) simultaneously forces both endpoint coefficients to1/3. The combined coefficient matrix has rank3 and augmented rank4. The instructed solver has no solution even at this fixed mesh size.

Interpreting the rectangular system as least squares changes the problem: the interior coefficient becomes11/18. The actual constrained finite-dimensional minimum has interior coefficient7/12 and strictly smaller objective; their objective difference is exactly1/3888. Omitting the boundary test rows correctly repairs this finite quadratic problem, but it does not create the missing continuous minimizer. Refining that repaired discretization approaches the unconstrained local GP in L2, with an inadmissible trace limit and diverging derivative norm, rather than the asserted trace-constrained solution.

AppendixB does not resolve either difficulty. The nonzero-boundary set is affine, rather than the Hilbert vector space claimed there. Even for homogeneous traces, L2 coercivity is not H1 coercivity or completeness in the L2 norm. This report does not claim that nonexistence alone refutes Proposition2's literal equivalence: both sides of an equivalence may be empty. It refutes the subsequent solvability and convergence construction and supplies a direct inconsistent-system certificate.

The author's current code page links a Version2 archive explicitly associated with this JMLR paper, copyright2018. Its source uses pseudoinverses or selected inverse rows to obtain outputs despite the published inconsistency. An unmodified native Octave run of its two-dimensional assembly and solver on a small squared-exponential GP has full-row residual0.04665 and a nonzero feasible objective derivative0.06979. Its objective is −0.09928 versus −0.11142 for the exactly solved constrained quadratic. This is corroboration that returning a numerical array does not solve the stated equations or minimization. The archive's identity to the historical2016 implementation has not been established, and no published experiment or table is claimed reproduced or numerically falsified by this source check.

**Reason for rejection.** A solvable variational formulation and a convergent finite-element boundary solver are the principal methodological advance over the preceding DDM method. For admissible GP covariances and boundary estimates the target solution does not exist, and the explicit computational equations are inconsistent. Merely correcting an affine test-space statement or selecting a least-squares solution cannot restore this contribution. A finite-mesh heuristic may still give continuous predictions, but presenting it as such withdraws the proposed continuum solution and convergence claim; adding a derivative/RKHS penalty or another boundary-coupling objective changes the central formulation and requires new analysis. This finding does not claim that finite-mesh continuity, useful empirical performance, or the ordinary unconstrained GP identities are false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the boundary constraints from the objective to AppendixB, noticed that the energy has an L2 mass term but no term controlling derivatives or traces. The subsequent full-row mass equations appeared incompatible with independently prescribed boundary values.

**Verification method.** Read all29 PDF pages, including both appendices, and rechecked the original rendered definition, equations, solver instructions and convergence assertion. Constructed the explicit feasible boundary-layer sequence, completed the square, and verified the finite-element rank contradiction and objective gap with exact rational arithmetic. Repeated the nonattainment argument with the paper's exponential covariance and its own boundary-estimation rule. Checked repaired finite-QP refinements and inspected and ran the authentic current-linked author source with provenance and historical limitations recorded.

**Confidence.** High. Nonattainment and the rank contradiction are exact consequences of the stated objective and equations; they do not rely on a failed optimizer, unavailable historical results, or a conjectural counterexample.

The instructed solver has no solution even at this fixed mesh size.

Interpreting the rectangular system as least squares changes the problem: the interior coefficient becomes11/18. The actual constrained finite-dimensional minimum has interior coefficient7/12 and strictly smaller objective; their objective difference is exactly1/3888. Omitting the boundary test rows correctly repairs this finite quadratic problem, but it does not create the missing continuous minimizer. Refining that repaired discretization approaches the unconstrained local GP in L2, with an inadmissible trace limit and diverging derivative norm, rather than the asserted trace-constrained solution.

AppendixB does not resolve either difficulty. The nonzero-boundary set is affine, rather than the Hilbert vector space claimed there. Even for homogeneous traces, L2 coercivity is not H1 coercivity or completeness in the L2 norm. This report does not claim that nonexistence alone refutes Proposition2's literal equivalence: both sides of an equivalence may be empty. It refutes the subsequent solvability and convergence construction and supplies a direct inconsistent-system certificate.

The author's current code page links a Version2 archive explicitly associated with this JMLR paper, copyright2018. Its source uses pseudoinverses or selected inverse rows to obtain outputs despite the published inconsistency. Constructed the explicit feasible boundary-layer sequence, completed the square, and verified the finite-element rank contradiction and objective gap with exact rational arithmetic. Repeated the nonattainment argument with the paper's exponential covariance and its own boundary-estimation rule. Checked repaired finite-QP refinements and inspected and ran the authentic current-linked author source with provenance and historical limitations recorded.

findings.title: Smooth target boundaries do not give the claimed logarithmic regret or fast expected approachability rate
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-339__I01 — Smooth target boundaries do not give the claimed logarithmic regret or fast expected approachability rate
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page13, Proposition12 and Equations14–15; proof on pages13–15, especially the treatment of entries into and exits from S at the bottom of14 and top of15. The fast-rate contribution is introduced on page3, reiterated on15 and identified as new on18. The underlying randomized-reward model and Blackwell strategy are defined on4–5; page10 separately identifies the smoothed-payoff variant in Remark9.

**Claim.** Under Assumption1—a compact convex target S whose unique outer unit normal is κ₀-Lipschitz on its smooth boundary—Blackwell’s algorithm of Theorem2 has, whenever its current average is outside S, the FTL regret bound a(T)=C₀(1+lnT), with C₀=diam(R)·||R−S||₂·κ₀. Consequently Proposition12 asserts

    E[d(bar_r_T,S)] <= C₀(1+ln T)/T   for every T>=1.

Here the paper’s Definition1 uses bar_r_T=T^(-1)sum_t r(i_t,j_t), the average of actual sampled pure-action rewards. No restriction to pure responses, strict interior feasibility or smoothed rewards is imposed in Proposition12.

**Error and evidence.** Both conclusions fail under the printed assumptions. The following two examples use the same smooth target and constants; they show respectively the wrong expected rate and the broken FTL-regret argument.

Take dimension2, e₁=(1,0), and the closed unit disk S={s:||s||₂<=1}. Its boundary is smooth, and its outer normal is n(s)=s, so κ₀=1 satisfies Assumption1 exactly. In both games below the reward set is R=[0,2]e₁. Thus diam(R)=2, max_{r∈R,s∈S}||r−s||₂=3, and the proposition’s constant is C₀=6.

1. **The expected distance is of order T^(-1/2), rather than log(T)/T.** Let both players have two actions, with vector reward matrix

       [[0*e₁, 2*e₁],
        [2*e₁, 0*e₁]].

   Use the mixed response x=(1/2,1/2) at every round, with independent fresh randomization. This is a valid response for every direction w: for either Nature action j, r(x,j)=e₁∈S and

       <w,r(x,j)>=w₁ <= ||w||₂ = h_S(w).

   Therefore it satisfies the Blackwell separation condition on page5, including every direction chosen from the current actual average. When that average lies in S, Theorem2 explicitly permits an arbitrary action, so the same mixed response is allowed. It is also a valid minimax response for the scalarized two-column game. The target is approachable: against every nonanticipating Nature strategy these rewards have conditional mean e₁ and bounded martingale differences, so the average converges uniformly in probability, and almost surely, to e₁∈S.

   Now let Nature always choose its first action. The realized rewards are iid0 or2 times e₁ with equal probabilities. With K~Binomial(T,1/2),

       bar_r_T=(2K/T)e₁,
       d(bar_r_T,S)=max(0,2K−T)/T.

   For even T=2m, direct binomial summation gives the exact expectation

       E[d(bar_r_T,S)] = binom(2m,m)/2^(2m+1).

   To verify the identity, use (k−m)binom(2m,k)=m[binom(2m−1,k−1)−binom(2m−1,k)] and telescope over k>m. The expression is asymptotic to1/sqrt(2πT), so no change to the finite constant C₀ can give the claimed order.

   There is also a finite exact contradiction at T=100000. The expectation is approximately.00126156310710; the printed bound6(1+ln100000)/100000 is approximately.000750775527898. This does not depend on rounded numerical integration or Monte Carlo. The control script verifies the integer inequality

       50000*binom(100000,50000) > 78*2^100000.

   Hence the exact expectation exceeds78/100000. Meanwhile exp(12)>sum_{k=0}^{20}12^k/k!>100000, so ln100000<12 and the claimed bound is strictly below78/100000.

2. **The asserted FTL-regret bound already fails with pure deterministic rewards.** This second game has one Nature action and two agent actions: low gives0, high gives2e₁. Choose high whenever the previous average is in S, including its boundary, and choose low whenever it is outside. This is a valid pure Blackwell strategy: outside S all reachable averages point in direction e₁, and low satisfies <e₁,0><=h_S(e₁)=1; inside S arbitrary actions are explicitly allowed. Start with high.

   The rewards are deterministically2e₁,0,2e₁,0,... . With the paper’s prescribed FTL choice w=0 inside S, the steering vectors are0 on odd rounds and e₁ on even rounds. At T=101, the average is(102/101)e₁, strictly outside S. For f_t(w)=−<w,r_t>+||w||₂,

       sum_t f_t(w_t)=50,
       min_{||w||₂<=1} sum_t f_t(w)=−1,
       Regret_101=51.

   Yet6(1+ln101) is approximately33.6907, and is strictly below36 because exp5>sum_{k=0}^{9}5^k/k!>101. This violates the very regret bound Proposition12 states for an outside endpoint. At general odd T=2m+1 this regret is m+1, so the error is linear versus logarithmic. This example has no randomization or distinction between actual and bilinear expected rewards.

The unsupported proof step is the extension across visits to S. The bottom of page14 replaces a block by f_k(w_k)−f_m(w_{m+1}), and page15 attempts to control that block by the change in the steering direction. These are different functions, with different stage rewards. In the deterministic example, the block k=2,m=3 has w_k=w_{m+1}=e₁, so the direction change is zero, but f_k(w_k)−f_m(w_{m+1})=1−(−1)=2. Repeated crossings accumulate this positive cost.

The paper contains a notation inconsistency worth separating from this counterexample: Section3.2 and Algorithm1 write r_t=r(x_t,j_t), whereas Lemma6/Theorem7 then explicitly analyze r(i_t,j_t) and a martingale correction. Rechecking pages4–5/9–10/12–15 confirms that Proposition12 invokes the actual-reward Blackwell algorithm of Theorem2 and states an expected distance, with no Remark9 restriction. The first example refutes that stated actual-reward conclusion. For the *different* smoothed-payoff problem of Remark9, its payoff is always e₁ and its distance is zero; no failure of that narrower performance quantity is asserted. The second counterexample refutes the FTL claim even under a smoothed-payoff reading.

**Reason for rejection.** The fast smooth-target convergence result is an explicit central theoretical contribution: the introduction distinguishes it from the known T^(-1/2) rate, Section4.1 presents it as a new logarithmic-regret analysis, and page18 singles out the faster expected distance as new. A compact smooth disk does not remove the T^(-1/2) fluctuation in actual randomized rewards, and even the proposed logarithmic FTL bound fails for an allowed pure strategy. These are exact false conclusions, rather than merely an incomplete proof. Increasing a constant, repairing an index, or correcting the mixed-versus-actual notation cannot restore the claimed rates. Obtaining a valid fast theorem requires substantive additional restrictions or a different performance quantity/strategy, and a new argument for crossings. The general support-function construction and the usual regularized T^(-1/2) approachability theory can remain valid; they do not validate this advertised new result. The false central rate would justify rejecting the paper as written.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the claimed smooth-boundary improvement, compared its expected-distance order with fluctuations of actual mixed-action rewards, then inspected the proof’s treatment of repeated boundary crossings.

**Verification method.** Read the complete23-page paper, including AppendixA. Rechecked full rendered pages containing the model, theorem, mixed/smoothed distinction and crossing argument. Constructed the two finite games, verified every smoothness/approachability/response assumption, derived the binomial expectation and deterministic regret exactly, checked integer inequalities and small-horizon binomial enumerations, and obtained a separate bounded original-PDF/algebra audit. No simulated or historical empirical results are used.

**Confidence: High.** The finite contradictions satisfy the printed assumptions, use the paper’s own constant6, and are certified by integer arithmetic. The separate pure-reward example removes the main interpretation ambiguity; the stochastic example establishes a different asymptotic rate, not only an incorrect constant.

findings.title: The two-stage precision estimator has a dimension-dependent bias larger than its claimed rate
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-345__I01 — The two-stage precision estimator has a dimension-dependent bias larger than its claimed rate
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages10–11, Theorems3.3–3.4 and Equations(3.6)–(3.9); PDF pages12–13, the two-stage algorithm; PDF page28, proof of Theorem3.3. The optimal inverse-covariance claim also appears in the abstract/PDF1 and contributions/PDF7. PDF page10 is printed journal page354, and PDF page28 is printed372.

**Claim.** Under B0–B2—sub-Gaussian observations, at most `s` nonzero off-diagonal entries of the true precision, and uniformly bounded positive precision eigenvalues—the paper's estimator first regularizes the sample correlation matrix, inverts that estimate, and regularizes the inverse. With penalties of order `sqrt(log(p)/n)` in the stated admissible positive-definiteness regions, Theorem3.3 claims Frobenius error `O_P(sqrt(s log(p)/n))` for inverse correlation and operator error `O_P(sqrt((s+1)log(p)/n))` for precision. Theorem3.4 gives the analogous direct-covariance two-stage precision estimator Frobenius rate `O_P(sqrt((s+p)log(p)/n))`.

**Error and evidence.** Entrywise thresholding the covariance before inversion creates a systematic error that precision sparsity does not control. The following Gaussian sequence satisfies the stated assumptions and tuning constraints but violates all these precision rates.

Let `k→∞`, `m=k²`, `p=m+1`, and `a=1/(2k)`. Index one center by0 and the other `m` coordinates as leaves. Define the true correlation/covariance matrix by

```
R00 = Rii = 1,
R0i = Ri0 = -a,
Rij = a²                 (distinct leaves i,j).
```

Its inverse is exactly

```
Ω00 = [1+(m-1)a²]/(1-a²),
Ω0i = Ωi0 = a/(1-a²),
Ωii = 1/(1-a²),
Ωij = 0                  (distinct leaves i,j).
```

Thus B1 holds with `s=2m`. On the leaf subspace orthogonal to the all-ones vector, `R` has eigenvalue `1-a²`. On the remaining two-dimensional subspace it is

```
[ 1       -1/2          ]
[ -1/2    5/4-1/(4m)   ].
```

Both this block and its inverse have all eigenvalues strictly between `1/2` and2. Consequently B2 holds with a fixed constant2. Taking observations iid `N(0,R)` gives B0, unit marginal variances, and no non-Gaussian or ill-conditioning exception.

Set every first- and second-stage penalty `λ=γ=δ=p⁻²` and `n=ceil(p⁴ log(p))`. Then `δ~sqrt(log(p)/n)` and `(s+p)log(p)/n→0`. First evaluate the estimator at its population covariance `R`; the Gaussian sampling argument below transfers the result to the stated empirical estimator.

For large `k`, all off-diagonal entries exceed the threshold in absolute value. The first-stage estimate has diagonal1, center-leaf entry

```
b = (-a+δ/2)/(1+δ),
```

and distinct-leaf entry

```
c = (a²-δ/2)/(1+δ).
```

Put `v=1+(m-1)c`, `D=v-mb²`, and let `A` be its inverse. Elementary block inversion gives

```
A00 = v/D,
Aii = 1/(1-c) + (b²-c)/[(1-c)D].
```

Write `t=tr(A)/p`. Because the second-stage ℓ1 penalty excludes the diagonal, its exact center diagonal is

```
Z00 = (A00+δt)/(1+δ).
```

Substitution and rational simplification yield the exact limit

```
(Z00-Ω00)/(mδ) → 1/8.
```

For a shorter derivation, let `u=(-1,1,…,1)^T`. The first-stage error is

```
Δ = [γ(I-R) + (λ/2)I - (λ/2)uu^T]/(1+γ).
```

The inverse expansion has center entry `(λ/2)(Ωu)0²+O(δ)+O((pδ)²)`. Here `(Ωu)0/k→1/2`, so the leading term is `mδ/8`; the other terms are smaller. The second-stage diagonal shrinkage changes it by only `O(δ)`. This also shows that replacing the penalties by any fixed positive constant multiples of `δ` retains the failure; increasing the first threshold's constant cannot repair the rate.

The diagonal error alone lower-bounds both Frobenius and operator error. Yet the claimed rate is of order `sqrt(m)δ`. Its ratio to the demonstrated error diverges as `sqrt(m)/(8sqrt(2))`. Exact fraction arithmetic and symbolic limits reproduce the result; at `p=250001` the center diagonal error alone is43.75 times `sqrt(s)δ`, and this ratio continues to grow. This is a failure of the asserted order, rather than a missing constant.

The tuning constraints do not exclude the construction. Every symmetric sign matrix has operator norm at most `p`; hence the first admissibility matrix has minimum eigenvalue at least `λmin(R)+δ-pδ/2`, uniformly positive. The same bound applies to the inverse input at the second stage. The paper writes “for every ε>0” in these regions, which literally makes them empty. Even under the intended, more favorable interpretation requiring positivity above a fixed small ε, the present tuning is admissible uniformly. The counterexample does not rely on that quantifier typo.

Finally, for the actual iid Gaussian sample, centered sample covariance and correlation satisfy `||K-R||op=O_P(sqrt(p/n))`. This follows, for example, by applying a finite sphere net to Gaussian quadratic-form concentration; bounded eigenvalues and diagonal normalization preserve this order. In this sequence it is `o(1/p)`, so with probability tending to1 the first-stage signs and nonzero threshold branches agree with the population ones. The first threshold map is then affine in `K`, and inversion is uniformly Lipschitz because the eigenvalues stay bounded away from0. Only the center diagonal and normalized trace are needed at the second stage, so no operator-Lipschitz assertion about entrywise thresholding is required. Their perturbations are `O_P(sqrt(p/n))=o(sqrt(p)δ)`. Rescaling by the sample marginal variance to obtain precision introduces a still smaller center-diagonal perturbation. Therefore the actual empirical estimator has the same `mδ/8` leading bias with probability tending to1, contradicting the `O_P(sqrt(p)δ)` bounds. The direct-covariance version has the same population matrix and conclusion.

The proof's unsupported step is visible on PDF28: it replaces a trace containing left and right inverse matrices by their spectral bounds times `|tr((Rhat-R0)Δ)|`. Such a bound on a signed trace does not follow from spectral bounds and loses the dense covariance bias amplified in this example.

**Reason for rejection.** Optimal-rate estimation under precision sparsity is an explicit central contribution. The claimed rate fails on a uniformly well-conditioned Gaussian star precision model satisfying B0–B2, even with feasible tuning and vanishing error. Repair requires changing the first-stage estimator/tuning theory or adding a substantive covariance-structure restriction; precision sparsity alone is insufficient. A constant correction or a repaired trace inequality cannot restore the stated theorem for this estimator. The covariance-only results and historical empirical scores are not asserted false by this finding, but the advertised inverse-covariance optimality is invalid as written.

**Discovery method.** Traced the precision-rate proof to the covariance estimator it inverts and noticed that the proof uses covariance error as though it inherited the precision sparsity pattern. A sparse star precision gives an analytically invertible covariance with a dense leaf block, exposing the mismatch.

**Verification method.** Rechecked all28 pages and the original rendered theorem/algorithm/proof pages for added covariance-sparsity assumptions, tuning exclusions, diagonal penalties, or alternative first-stage rules. Derived the block inverses exactly, verified the limit with rational arithmetic/SymPy, checked the uniform eigenvalue and tuning bounds, and justified transfer to iid Gaussian samples. Native R evaluation of the full paper formulas agrees with the block formulas to below `9e-16` at `p=26,101,226,401`. An independent bounded reviewer also checked the original assumptions and sample-transfer argument. The authentic2015 JPEN package was inspected: its standalone inverse function bypasses the first covariance stage on positive-definite input, so no claim is made that its raw-input path or the published empirical experiments suffer this particular failure.

**Confidence.** High. The covariance and inverse, sparsity, spectral bounds, feasible penalties, and divergent rate ratio are explicit. The sample-transfer argument uses only uniformly well-conditioned inversion and the estimator's diagonal formula; it does not depend on unavailable historical code, failed reruns, or an unproved claim that a numerical optimizer found a global solution.

Reproduction artifacts: exact derivation and controls, results, Gaussian sample-law checks, and independent bounded QA.

Ωij = 0                  (distinct leaves i,j).

Thus B1 holds with \(s=2m\). On the leaf subspace orthogonal to the all-ones vector, \(R\) has eigenvalue \(1-a^{2}\). On the remaining two-dimensional subspace it is

[ 1       -1/2          ]
[ -1/2    5/4-1/(4m)   ].

Both this block and its inverse have all eigenvalues strictly between \(\frac{1}{2}\) and2. Consequently B2 holds with a fixed constant2. Taking observations iid \(N(0,R)\) gives B0, unit marginal variances, and no non-Gaussian or ill-conditioning exception.

Set every first- and second-stage penalty \(\lambda =\gamma =\delta =p^{-2}\) and \(n=\operatorname{ceil}(p^{4} \log (p))\). Then \(\delta \sim \operatorname{sqrt}(\log (p)/n)\) and \((s+p)\log (p)/n\to 0\). First evaluate the estimator at its population covariance \(R\); the Gaussian sampling argument below transfers the result to the stated empirical estimator.

For large \(k\), all off-diagonal entries exceed the threshold in absolute value. The first-stage estimate has diagonal1, center-leaf entry

b = (-a+δ/2)/(1+δ),

and distinct-leaf entry

c = (a²-δ/2)/(1+δ).

Put \(v=1+(m-1)c\), D=v-mb², and let \(A\) be its inverse. Elementary block inversion gives

A00 = v/D,
Aii = 1/(1-c) + (b²-c)/[(1-c)D].

Write \(t=\operatorname{tr}(A)/p\). Because the second-stage ℓ1 penalty excludes the diagonal, its exact center diagonal is

Z00 = (A00+δt)/(1+δ).

Substitution and rational simplification yield the exact limit

(Z00-Ω00)/(mδ) → 1/8.

For a shorter derivation, let \(u=(-1,1,\ldots ,1)^{T}\). The first-stage error is

Δ = [γ(I-R) + (λ/2)I - (λ/2)uu^T]/(1+γ).

The inverse expansion has center entry (λ/2)(Ωu)0²+O(δ)+O((pδ)²). Here (Ωu)0/k→1/2, so the leading term is \(m\delta /8\); the other terms are smaller. The second-stage diagonal shrinkage changes it by only \(O(\delta )\). This also shows that replacing the penalties by any fixed positive constant multiples of \(\delta\) retains the failure; increasing the first threshold's constant cannot repair the rate.

The diagonal error alone lower-bounds both Frobenius and operator error. Yet the claimed rate is of order \(\operatorname{sqrt}(m)\delta\). Its ratio to the demonstrated error diverges as \(\operatorname{sqrt}(m)/(8\operatorname{sqrt}(2))\). Exact fraction arithmetic and symbolic limits reproduce the result; at \(p=250001\) the center diagonal error alone is43.75 times \(\operatorname{sqrt}(s)\delta\), and this ratio continues to grow. This is a failure of the asserted order, rather than a missing constant.

The tuning constraints do not exclude the construction. Every symmetric sign matrix has operator norm at most \(p\); hence the first admissibility matrix has minimum eigenvalue at least \(\lambda \min (R)+\delta -p\delta /2\), uniformly positive. The same bound applies to the inverse input at the second stage. The paper writes “for every ε>0” in these regions, which literally makes them empty. Even under the intended, more favorable interpretation requiring positivity above a fixed small ε, the present tuning is admissible uniformly. The counterexample does not rely on that quantifier typo.

Finally, for the actual iid Gaussian sample, centered sample covariance and correlation satisfy ||K-R||op=O_P(sqrt(p/n)). This follows, for example, by applying a finite sphere net to Gaussian quadratic-form concentration; bounded eigenvalues and diagonal normalization preserve this order. In this sequence it is \(o(1/p)\), so with probability tending to1 the first-stage signs and nonzero threshold branches agree with the population ones. The first threshold map is then affine in \(K\), and inversion is uniformly Lipschitz because the eigenvalues stay bounded away from0. Only the center diagonal and normalized trace are needed at the second stage, so no operator-Lipschitz assertion about entrywise thresholding is required. Their perturbations are \(O_{P}(\operatorname{sqrt}(p/n))=o(\operatorname{sqrt}(p)\delta )\). Rescaling by the sample marginal variance to obtain precision introduces a still smaller center-diagonal perturbation. Therefore the actual empirical estimator has the same \(m\delta /8\) leading bias with probability tending to1, contradicting the \(O_{P}(\operatorname{sqrt}(p)\delta )\) bounds. The direct-covariance version has the same population matrix and conclusion.

The proof's unsupported step is visible on PDF28: it replaces a trace containing left and right inverse matrices by their spectral bounds times |tr((Rhat-R0)Δ)|. Such a bound on a signed trace does not follow from spectral bounds and loses the dense covariance bias amplified in this example.

Reason for rejection. Optimal-rate estimation under precision sparsity is an explicit central contribution. The claimed rate fails on a uniformly well-conditioned Gaussian star precision model satisfying B0–B2, even with feasible tuning and vanishing error. Repair requires changing the first-stage estimator/tuning theory or adding a substantive covariance-structure restriction; precision sparsity alone is insufficient. A constant correction or a repaired trace inequality cannot restore the stated theorem for this estimator. The covariance-only results and historical empirical scores are not asserted false by this finding, but the advertised inverse-covariance optimality is invalid as written.

Discovery method. Traced the precision-rate proof to the covariance estimator it inverts and noticed that the proof uses covariance error as though it inherited the precision sparsity pattern. A sparse star precision gives an analytically invertible covariance with a dense leaf block, exposing the mismatch.

Verification method. Rechecked all28 pages and the original rendered theorem/algorithm/proof pages for added covariance-sparsity assumptions, tuning exclusions, diagonal penalties, or alternative first-stage rules. Derived the block inverses exactly, verified the limit with rational arithmetic/SymPy, checked the uniform eigenvalue and tuning bounds, and justified transfer to iid Gaussian samples. Native R evaluation of the full paper formulas agrees with the block formulas to below \(9\times10^{-16}\) at \(p=26,101,226,401\). An independent bounded reviewer also checked the original assumptions and sample-transfer argument. The authentic2015 JPEN package was inspected: its standalone inverse function bypasses the first covariance stage on positive-definite input, so no claim is made that its raw-input path or the published empirical experiments suffer this particular failure.

Confidence. High. The covariance and inverse, sparsity, spectral bounds, feasible penalties, and divergent rate ratio are explicit. The sample-transfer argument uses only uniformly well-conditioned inversion and the estimator's diagonal formula; it does not depend on unavailable historical code, failed reruns, or an unproved claim that a numerical optimizer found a global solution.

Reproduction artifacts: exact derivation and controls, results, Gaussian sample-law checks, and independent bounded QA.

findings.title: The central finite-step Fisher/Wilks proof incorrectly treats a block iterate as a profile maximizer
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-392__I01 — The central finite-step Fisher/Wilks proof incorrectly treats a block iterate as a profile maximizer
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 37, Lemma 34, Equations (37)–(38), and the displayed tilted-path maximization/zero-efficient-score step in its proof; PDF page 17, Theorem 7, Equations (21)–(23) and its iteration prescription; PDF page 38, Corollary 13 proof. The advertised finite-step statistical contribution appears on PDF 1 and 4–6.

**Claim.** Theorem 7 says that, on an event of probability at least 1−8exp(−x)−beta, every finite iterate theta_k has Fisher and profile-likelihood expansion errors bounded by the semiparametric spread. Its spread (21) is weak_epsilon times a fixed expression in r_k and the concentration parameters; the radius r_k is at most a constant times sqrt(p*+x)+nu^k R0. Thus the computational contraction term appears only inside a quantity multiplied by the curvature/stochastic-increment remainder constant. Lemma 34 is the step that asserts these same expansions for all k and supplies the first theorem's proof.

**Error and evidence.** A block iterate need not have zero efficient score. The proof defines

\[
l(\theta_1,\theta_2,\eta)
=L\{\theta_1,\eta+H^{-2}A^\top(\theta_2-\theta_1)\}.
\]

It then asserts that theta_k maximizes l(theta,theta_k,eta_k), and concludes that the efficient score

\[
\breve\nabla L(\theta_k,\eta_k)
=\nabla_\theta L(\theta_k,\eta_k)-AH^{-2}\nabla_\eta L(\theta_k,\eta_k)
\]

is zero. The algorithm gives only the first raw partial score equal to zero at this pair. The nuisance block was optimized at the preceding theta value.

This fails exactly in the paper's own Gaussian-quadratic example class. Let p=m=1,

\[
Q=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
Y\sim N(0,Q^{-1}),\quad
L(v,Y)=-\tfrac12(v-Y)^\top Q(v-Y).
\]

Take the initial guess v_0=(0,0), which equals the population target. The information matrix is Q, its eigenvalues are 1/2 and 3/2, the block information values are D=H=1, A=1/2, and nu=1/4. All expected Hessian blocks are constant and the stochastic gradient is a random constant vector, so every Hessian/gradient-increment remainder in Lemma 34's weak smoothness and moment assumptions is zero. Their strictly positive epsilon constants can therefore be taken arbitrarily small; no zero-denominator convention is required.

The exact unique block maximizations give

\[
\eta_k=Y_\eta+\tfrac12(Y_\theta-\theta_{k-1}),\qquad
\theta_k=\tfrac34Y_\theta+\tfrac14\theta_{k-1}
=(1-4^{-k})Y_\theta.
\]

The full/profile maximizer is theta_hat=Y_theta. The efficient information and normalized efficient score are

\[
\breve D=\sqrt3/2,\qquad \breve\xi=(\sqrt3/2)Y_\theta\sim N(0,1).
\]

Consequently the actual finite-step errors are

\[
\breve D\theta_k-\breve\xi=-4^{-k}\breve\xi,
\]

\[
\max_\eta L(\theta_k,\eta)-\max_\eta L(0,\eta)
-\tfrac12\breve\xi^2=-\tfrac12\,16^{-k}\breve\xi^2.
\]

These computational errors do not vanish when the local Taylor/increment remainder is zero. They cannot be bounded by a spread that can be made arbitrarily small solely by selecting valid smaller smoothness constants.

For a finite exact witness set the realized Y=(1,0). At k=1 the algorithm gives (theta_1,eta_1)=(3/4,1/2), with raw gradient (0,−3/8). Its efficient score is 3/16, rather than zero. The proof's tilted one-dimensional function is uniquely maximized at theta=1, rather than theta_1=3/4. The Fisher error is sqrt(3)/8 and the profile-Wilks error is 3/128.

The event/localization terms do not explain this away. With x=10, b=1/2, epsilon=weak_epsilon=10^-14, and all increment variance proxies equal to 1, the paper's explicit formulas give C(nu)=64 sqrt(2), R0=61.55323, z=8.24621, and the Equation (33) upper radius r_1=2885.51717. The spread (21), even evaluated at this generous upper radius, is 1.06102e−5. The actual Fisher error is 0.216506, and the actual Wilks error 0.0234375 exceeds Theorem 7's corresponding right-hand side 4.59440e−5. All standardized scores at the witness are at most 1, every block iterate and the relevant maximizers lie within radius 2, the stochastic increment processes vanish, and initialization condition A1 holds identically with K0=beta=0. Thus the witness belongs to the defined desirable event, as does an open neighborhood. This directly falsifies Lemma 34 under its stated weak assumptions and event.

The probabilistic problem is substantial. For the explicit radius above, the first Fisher bound can hold only if |xi| is at most four times 1.06102e−5. Since xi is standard normal, its probability is at most 3.3863e−5, compared with the first main theorem's advertised 0.9996368 at x=10. More generally, take n iid observations from N(0,Q^-1) and their usual log likelihood. Starting at the truth still gives K0=0, while xi remains standard normal and the finite-k errors above remain unchanged in normalized coordinates. One may take epsilon=weak_epsilon=n^-1/2; R0 and the claimed radius bound remain bounded for fixed x and k. The claimed spread then tends to zero, while the actual errors do not. This argument defeats any fixed allowed radius constant.

There is a separate sign typo in the printed full-model condition L0 on PDF 14: it compares the expected Hessian, rather than its negative, to the positive information matrix. Taken literally as r tends to zero, that condition is impossible. This report does not exploit that typo or call a vacuous literal implication false. The direct counterexample is to Lemma 34, whose weak assumptions do not include the impossible full-model formula. Even after the favorable conventional sign correction, the first main finite-step guarantee fails by the Gaussian calculation above.

The iteration range was checked in the original: Theorem 7 and Lemma 34 both explicitly cover every k in N. The section heading “Result after Convergence” imposes no additional mathematical condition. The theorem's additional iteration prescription depends only on p*, x, R0 and nu; for this truth-start example it remains constant in n. No contraction error outside the spread or omitted lower bound on k repairs the stated result.

**Reason for rejection.** The first named contribution is a finite-sample Fisher/Wilks guarantee for the alternating sequence and an explicit answer to how many steps achieve the profile estimator's statistical accuracy. Its essential proof step is false, and its asserted accuracy fails even for an exactly quadratic, correctly specified, uniformly well-conditioned Gaussian likelihood started at the truth. A repair must retain a computational error outside the statistical remainder and change the required iteration budget: for example, matching an O(n^-1/2) Fisher remainder requires k at least log(n)/(2log 4)+O(1) in this model. This is not a constant or notation correction to the claimed finite-step result. The alternating sequence still converges geometrically, and the limiting MLE has the usual Fisher/Wilks properties; neither actual convergence nor every other theorem is claimed refuted.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Lemma 34's transfer of a profile-MLE proof to finite block iterates, noticed that the efficient-score stationarity condition is stronger than either available coordinate stationarity condition. The exactly quadratic limit of its spread exposed the missing computational error.

**Verification method.** Read all 53 PDF pages and all three appendices. Rechecked the algorithm, assumptions, spread, iteration range and tilted-path step in the rendered originals. Derived the Gaussian block recursion, efficient score and profile likelihood exactly; verified rational finite iterates and tilted maximization symbolically; checked the explicit event/radius/spread calculations and exact normal success probability. Additional independent matrix-block controls verify the surviving contraction and Schur-complement identities. An independent bounded reviewer checked selected original pages and re-derived the score, tilted maximizer, explicit radius, spread and normal probability; the scoped record is saved with the evidence. The paper has no empirical experiment whose failure is asserted.

**Confidence.** High. The false tilted maximization, nonzero efficient score and finite-step errors are explicit algebraic identities. The counterexample directly addresses Lemma 34's assumptions, and the separately printed full-model sign typo and surviving limiting/convergence results are disclosed.
