findings.title: The claimed exact marginal matching solver optimizes a different objective and returns a suboptimal matching
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-420__I01 — The claimed exact marginal matching solver optimizes a different objective and returns a suboptimal matching
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 7, Section 3.2, definition of MIM-Marginal; PDF page 13, Equations (8), (10)–(16); PDF page 14, Algorithm 2 and the first paragraph of Section 4.3 claiming Algorithms 1 and 2 are guaranteed to obtain best matched control groups. The relevant singleton justification is immediately above Algorithm 2 on PDF page 14. The contribution is introduced on PDF pages 1–3 and summarized on PDF pages 24–25.

**Claim.** For fixed treated group T, control pool C with |C|>|T|, categorical covariates and target control size N, MIM-Marginal minimizes

\[
J(S)=\sum_k I(t;X_k),\qquad S\subseteq C,\quad |S|=N.
\]

Algorithm 2 instead solves a mixed integer program minimizing q subject to the marginal inequalities

\[
q\ge\frac{S_m-1-A}{\max\{T_m,\alpha\}},
\]

the specified joint-to-marginal count constraints, and integer count/capacity constraints. It uses A approximately −0.47 and stops when the maximizing marginal bin is unique for every covariate. The paper claims this returns an optimal MIM-Marginal solution. Algorithm 4 is separately described as a heuristic; that qualification is not applied to Algorithm 2.

**Error and evidence.** Consider two categorical covariates with 2 and 3 values. Rows and columns index these values. The following arrays specify numbers of individual treated and available control units in each joint bin:

\[
T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&2\\1&3&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
C=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&3\\3&2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad N=7.
\]

There are 7 treated units and 10 available controls, so the required strict pool-size inequality holds, and N equals the treated size. Every treated marginal count is positive:

\[
T_m=(3,4;\ 1,4,2).
\]

Thus the denominator replacement by alpha and conventions for empty treated marginal bins are irrelevant. Zero joint cells are allowed by the paper's count formulation.

With A=−0.47, the first MIP, with its forbidden set empty, has the unique solution

\[
S_{\rm bad}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&3\\1&2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
S_{{\rm bad},m}=(4,3;\ 1,3,3),\qquad q=247/200.
\]

To verify uniqueness without relying on a solver, any matching with q≤247/200 has at most 1 control in column 1: two would give (2−.53)/1=1.47>1.235. Columns 2 and 3 each have available capacity 3. Their total capacity with column 1 is 7, so selecting 7 controls forces column totals (1,3,3). This fixes the counts in columns 2 and 3 at their full capacities. Row 1 already contains 4 controls; adding the available control in its first cell would give (5−.53)/3=1.49>1.235. Hence its first cell is 0, and the entire displayed matching is forced. A lower q is impossible because it would prohibit 3 controls in column 3 and leave total capacity at most 6.

The five ratios for this solution are

\[
\left(\frac{347}{300},\frac{247}{400};\
\frac{47}{100},\frac{247}{400},\frac{247}{200}\right).
\]

The maximum is unique globally and within each covariate. Algorithm 2 therefore terminates immediately and returns this matching. No tie-breaking, forbidden-bin update, approximate MIP solution or time limit is involved. The inequalities remain strict for every A in [−.48,−.46].

However, the matching

\[
S_{\rm good}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&2\\2&2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
S_{{\rm good},m}=(3,4;\ 2,3,2)
\]

is feasible and has smaller objective J. Every cell is a nonnegative integer bounded by the corresponding cell of C, and the total is 7. Compute J using the paper's exact Equation (2). At fixed group sizes, write

\[
\phi(s,t)=s\log s+t\log t-(s+t)\log(s+t),\quad0\log0=0.
\]

The constants in Equation (2) cancel between matchings. Summing phi over all five marginal bins gives the exact certificate

\[
\exp\!\left(14[J(S_{\rm bad})-J(S_{\rm good})]\right)
=\frac{2282521714753536}{2119447102653125}>1.
\]

With natural logs, J(S_bad)=0.02254986863 and J(S_good)=0.01725518342, a strict gap 0.00529468521. Any other common log base preserves the inequality. Exhaustive exact-rational comparison of all 24 feasible cell-count assignments confirms that S_good is the unique true-MI optimum.

This failure is more than an inaccurate approximation of the paper's single-bin cost. As a preserving-repair check, replace its ratio by the **exact** marginal removal cost. Its exponent for positive counts is

\[
E(s,t)=\exp[\phi(s,t)-\phi(s-1,t)].
\]

Exhaustively minimizing max_m E(S_m,T_m) over the same 24 feasible matchings again uniquely selects S_bad. Its maximum is 1728/3125, whereas S_good's is 16/27. Thus correcting the earlier contour/ratio approximation still does not turn this marginal minimax criterion into the required sum of mutual informations. Both covariates change between the matchings; the certificate does not rely on improving an isolated marginal distribution while leaving the other unchanged.

**Reason for rejection.** An advertised central contribution is a tractable exact optimization method for the nonlinear MI matching objective. Algorithm 2 fails that central guarantee on a small admissible instance, even with an exact solution of its MIP and an unambiguous stopping decision. The unique-bin argument does not justify replacing a coupled sum of marginal MI terms by a maximum of marginal scores. Repairing a constant, adding solver precision or using exact single-bin costs leaves the counterexample. A valid exact solver requires a different global objective/formulation, or the paper must withdraw Algorithm 2's optimality guarantee and present it as another heuristic. This changes the claimed algorithmic contribution, rather than correcting a numerical constant or a proof line. The paper's MI balance measure and heuristic Algorithm 4 may remain useful; this finding does not assert that its historical empirical tables are false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the claimed optimality conditions, the reviewer noticed that Appendix B treats approximate contour linearity as exact. Small finite checks exposed false single-bin rankings. A first marginal witness shared that error, so the reviewer and a second auditor sought a stronger coupled witness. The final example above remains a counterexample after substituting exact single-bin removal costs.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the objective, constraints, categorical-count domain and stopping condition on the original rendered PDF pages 7, 13, 14, 16 and 27. Re-derived Equation (2)'s count form, enumerated all 24 feasible integer matchings with exact rational products, and independently solved the displayed linear-ratio MIP using native HiGHS: it returned S_bad and q=1.235. A second auditor independently read the relevant original pages and constructed the strengthened certificate. These are checks of the published algorithm, not a rerun of authentic historical author code or CPLEX experiment drivers, which were not recovered.

**Confidence: High.** The example satisfies the stated deterministic optimization conditions; the MIP optimum and stopping condition are unique; the MI gap is an exact integer inequality. Exact enumeration, an independent auditor and a native MILP solve agree. The finding is limited to the claimed exact marginal solver and does not infer unsupported empirical failures.
findings.html:
Exact location. PDF page 7, Section 3.2, definition of MIM-Marginal; PDF page 13, Equations (8), (10)–(16); PDF page 14, Algorithm 2 and the first paragraph of Section 4.3 claiming Algorithms 1 and 2 are guaranteed to obtain best matched control groups. The relevant singleton justification is immediately above Algorithm 2 on PDF page 14. The contribution is introduced on PDF pages 1–3 and summarized on PDF pages 24–25.

Claim. For fixed treated group T, control pool C with |C|>|T|, categorical covariates and target control size N, MIM-Marginal minimizes

\[ J(S)=\sum_k I(t;X_k),\qquad S\subseteq C,\quad |S|=N. \]

Algorithm 2 instead solves a mixed integer program minimizing q subject to the marginal inequalities

\[ q\ge\frac{S_m-1-A}{\max\{T_m,\alpha\}}, \]

the specified joint-to-marginal count constraints, and integer count/capacity constraints. It uses A approximately −0.47 and stops when the maximizing marginal bin is unique for every covariate. The paper claims this returns an optimal MIM-Marginal solution. Algorithm 4 is separately described as a heuristic; that qualification is not applied to Algorithm 2.

Error and evidence. Consider two categorical covariates with 2 and 3 values. Rows and columns index these values. The following arrays specify numbers of individual treated and available control units in each joint bin:

\[ T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&2\\1&3&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad C=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&3\\3&2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad N=7. \]

There are 7 treated units and 10 available controls, so the required strict pool-size inequality holds, and N equals the treated size. Every treated marginal count is positive:

\[ T_m=(3,4;\ 1,4,2). \]

Thus the denominator replacement by alpha and conventions for empty treated marginal bins are irrelevant. Zero joint cells are allowed by the paper's count formulation.

With A=−0.47, the first MIP, with its forbidden set empty, has the unique solution

\[ S_{\rm bad}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&3\\1&2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_{{\rm bad},m}=(4,3;\ 1,3,3),\qquad q=247/200. \]

To verify uniqueness without relying on a solver, any matching with q≤247/200 has at most 1 control in column 1: two would give (2−.53)/1=1.47>1.235. Columns 2 and 3 each have available capacity 3. Their total capacity with column 1 is 7, so selecting 7 controls forces column totals (1,3,3). This fixes the counts in columns 2 and 3 at their full capacities. Row 1 already contains 4 controls; adding the available control in its first cell would give (5−.53)/3=1.49>1.235. Hence its first cell is 0, and the entire displayed matching is forced. A lower q is impossible because it would prohibit 3 controls in column 3 and leave total capacity at most 6.

The five ratios for this solution are

\[ \left(\frac{347}{300},\frac{247}{400};\ \frac{47}{100},\frac{247}{400},\frac{247}{200}\right). \]

The maximum is unique globally and within each covariate. Algorithm 2 therefore terminates immediately and returns this matching. No tie-breaking, forbidden-bin update, approximate MIP solution or time limit is involved. The inequalities remain strict for every A in [−.48,−.46].

However, the matching

\[ S_{\rm good}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&2\\2&2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_{{\rm good},m}=(3,4;\ 2,3,2) \]

is feasible and has smaller objective J. Every cell is a nonnegative integer bounded by the corresponding cell of C, and the total is 7. Compute J using the paper's exact Equation (2). At fixed group sizes, write

\[ \phi(s,t)=s\log s+t\log t-(s+t)\log(s+t),\quad0\log0=0. \]

The constants in Equation (2) cancel between matchings. Summing phi over all five marginal bins gives the exact certificate

\[ \exp\!\left(14[J(S_{\rm bad})-J(S_{\rm good})]\right) =\frac{2282521714753536}{2119447102653125}>1. \]

With natural logs, J(S_bad)=0.02254986863 and J(S_good)=0.01725518342, a strict gap 0.00529468521. Any other common log base preserves the inequality. Exhaustive exact-rational comparison of all 24 feasible cell-count assignments confirms that S_good is the unique true-MI optimum.

This failure is more than an inaccurate approximation of the paper's single-bin cost. As a preserving-repair check, replace its ratio by the exact marginal removal cost. Its exponent for positive counts is

\[ E(s,t)=\exp[\phi(s,t)-\phi(s-1,t)]. \]

Exhaustively minimizing max_m E(S_m,T_m) over the same 24 feasible matchings again uniquely selects S_bad. Its maximum is 1728/3125, whereas S_good's is 16/27. Thus correcting the earlier contour/ratio approximation still does not turn this marginal minimax criterion into the required sum of mutual informations. Both covariates change between the matchings; the certificate does not rely on improving an isolated marginal distribution while leaving the other unchanged.

Reason for rejection. An advertised central contribution is a tractable exact optimization method for the nonlinear MI matching objective. Algorithm 2 fails that central guarantee on a small admissible instance, even with an exact solution of its MIP and an unambiguous stopping decision. The unique-bin argument does not justify replacing a coupled sum of marginal MI terms by a maximum of marginal scores. Repairing a constant, adding solver precision or using exact single-bin costs leaves the counterexample. A valid exact solver requires a different global objective/formulation, or the paper must withdraw Algorithm 2's optimality guarantee and present it as another heuristic. This changes the claimed algorithmic contribution, rather than correcting a numerical constant or a proof line. The paper's MI balance measure and heuristic Algorithm 4 may remain useful; this finding does not assert that its historical empirical tables are false.

Discovery method. While tracing the claimed optimality conditions, the reviewer noticed that Appendix B treats approximate contour linearity as exact. Small finite checks exposed false single-bin rankings. A first marginal witness shared that error, so the reviewer and a second auditor sought a stronger coupled witness. The final example above remains a counterexample after substituting exact single-bin removal costs.

Verification method. Rechecked the objective, constraints, categorical-count domain and stopping condition on the original rendered PDF pages 7, 13, 14, 16 and 27. Re-derived Equation (2)'s count form, enumerated all 24 feasible integer matchings with exact rational products, and independently solved the displayed linear-ratio MIP using native HiGHS: it returned S_bad and q=1.235. A second auditor independently read the relevant original pages and constructed the strengthened certificate. These are checks of the published algorithm, not a rerun of authentic historical author code or CPLEX experiment drivers, which were not recovered.

Confidence: High. The example satisfies the stated deterministic optimization conditions; the MIP optimum and stopping condition are unique; the MI gap is an exact integer inequality. Exact enumeration, an independent auditor and a native MILP solve agree. The finding is limited to the claimed exact marginal solver and does not infer unsupported empirical failures.

findings.title: The central uniform worst-case guarantee is false
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-440__I01 — The central uniform worst-case guarantee is false
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 8, Equation (9), defines the worst-case functional. Page 10, Lemma 1 and its spectral-norm interpretation, makes the supremum over response directions explicit. Page 11, Theorem 1, states the contradicted bound. The unsupported uniformity step is in Appendix B.1, page 22, using the structural condition (13) on page 20. The same underlying mistake recurs in Appendix B.3, pages 26–27. The resulting WC-versus-PE comparison is asserted in Sections 1.3 and 5, pages 5 and 17–18. All page numbers are original PDF page numbers.

**Claim.** For a fixed sketch, the paper defines

\[
C_{WC}(S)=\sup_Y\frac{\|Y-X\widehat\beta_S\|^2}
 {\|Y-X\widehat\beta_{OLS}\|^2}.
\]

Theorem 1 applies to any full-column-rank design and independent leverage sampling with replacement, with the stated diagonal rescaling. At exact leverage sampling, \(\theta=0\), it asserts \(C_{WC}(S)\le1+12p/r\) with probability at least 0.7 once \(r\ge Cp\log(C'p)\). The paper uses this uniform functional to conclude that WC and residual efficiency can be close to one at \(p\ll r\ll n\), while prediction efficiency scales as \(n/r\).

**Error and evidence.** Set \(p=1\) and \(X=\mathbf1_n\). This is full rank and has leverage scores \(\ell_i=1/n\), so the stated sampling law is exactly uniform. Let \(N_i\) be the number of times row \(i\) is drawn. For every realization, \(N_i\) are nonnegative integers, \(\sum_iN_i=r\), and \(SX\) has rank one. Rescaling is the same on every sampled row and cancels from the fitted coefficient:

\[
\widehat\beta_S=\sum_iw_iY_i,\qquad w_i=N_i/r,
\qquad \widehat\beta_{OLS}=n^{-1}\sum_iY_i.
\]

Choose the admissible response \(Y_i=w_i-1/n\). Its mean is zero. It is nonzero when \(r<n\), so the denominator is positive. Put \(d=\sum_i(w_i-1/n)^2\). Direct substitution gives \(\widehat\beta_{OLS}=0\), \(\widehat\beta_S=d\), and

\[
\frac{\|Y-X\widehat\beta_S\|^2}{\|Y-X\widehat\beta_{OLS}\|^2}
 =1+nd=n\sum_iw_i^2=\frac{n\sum_iN_i^2}{r^2}\ge\frac nr.
\]

The last inequality follows from \(N_i^2\ge N_i\). Cauchy–Schwarz on centered responses also shows that this chosen response attains the supremum, so the expression is exactly \(C_{WC}(S)\).

Choose any integer \(r\ge64\) large enough to satisfy the theorem's unspecified absolute-constant threshold, and set \(n=r^2\). Then every possible sketch has

\[
C_{WC}(S)\ge r>1+12/r.
\]

Thus the asserted success probability is **zero**, rather than at least 0.7. This family has \(r/n\to0\), uniform leverage, and no rank failure. It handles any fixed constants in the minimum-sample condition. The response may depend on the realized sketch because the paper expressly takes the supremum inside the fixed-sketch functional; this is precisely the distinction at issue.

There is a broader structural obstruction. For any rank-preserving sketch, complete \(U\) to an orthogonal basis \([U,V]\), and write

\[
(SU)^\dagger S=U^T+B V^T.
\]

The paper's own full-rank identities give

\[
C_{WC}(S)=1+\|B\|_{op}^2
\ \ge\ 1+\|B\|_F^2/p=C_{PE}(S).
\]

For \(p=1\) they are equal. In the counterexample, independent unit-variance Gaussian noise gives exactly \(C_{PE}(S)=n\sum_iN_i^2/r^2=C_{WC}(S)\). The proposed uniform-WC versus PE sample-complexity separation is therefore qualitatively impossible under the stated definitions.

Appendix B.1 bounds \(E_S\|U^TS^TS\epsilon\|^2\) for each fixed \(\epsilon\perp U\), then applies Markov's inequality for that fixed vector. This does not provide one event controlling all such vectors, as required by the supremum in Equation (13). Appendix B.3 makes the same passage explicitly. A valid pointwise-in-response probability bound cannot be substituted for this operator-norm event.

**Reason for rejection.** A central advertised contribution is a unified framework comparing three fixed-sketch performance criteria, with WC and RE behaving as \(p/r\) while PE behaves as \(n/r\). The defined WC functional instead dominates PE, and a main theorem fails for every sketch on the simplest uniform-leverage design. Changing numerical constants or adding a rank regularity condition cannot repair the discrepancy. Retaining the claim would require replacing the uniform objective and rewriting the structural conditions, theorem quantifiers, and comparative interpretation, or abandoning that central guarantee. This invalidates the paper's claimed rigorous three-way comparison as written and warrants rejection under the requested standard. The finding does **not** assert that all statistical PE/RE results are false. Recasting the algorithmic part as the usual guarantee for each fixed response could support a substantially revised paper; it does not prove the uniform result presented here.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the spectral-norm condition to the randomized proofs, I noticed that the proof only controlled a fixed residual vector. I then checked the one-column design to distinguish the two probability quantifiers.

**Verification method.** I reread all 31 pages, including Appendices A and B, and inspected the rendered definitions, theorem, supremum condition, and Markov steps. Exact rational arithmetic checked the directly fitted residual ratios for distinct samples, repeated samples, and the all-identical draw. Independent matrix calculations checked the general structural identity and an attaining response in 180 full-rank cases. A second auditor independently reread the relevant original pages and verified 200 sampled count vectors. These numerical controls supplement the exact all-realizations argument; they are not the basis for its probability claim.

 Results and bounded-review scope are under unpublished audit files. Figures 3 and 5 were also checked against the exact inequality. A fresh 20-case Gaussian-sketch calculation at the paper's \(n=1024,p=50,r=80,\nu=10\) settings yielded mean PE 35.053, true uniform WC 239.282, and RE 2.748. The published WC value 2.74 resembles RE, but the original code and raw draws were not recovered; I do not claim to have identified the historical computation or reproduced its 100 trials. This is one underlying uniformity error, not separate issues for each theorem or figure.

**Confidence.** High. The counterexample satisfies the sampling, rank, leverage, and dimension assumptions and fails for every sketch realization. The general inequality independently explains why the advertised scaling cannot hold for the defined criterion. The severity assessment specifically concerns the stated uniform framework and preserves the distinction from valid pointwise algorithmic guarantees.

findings.title: The spherical split and merge are not inverse reversible-jump moves
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-454__I01 — The spherical split and merge are not inverse reversible-jump moves
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages 11–13, Section 4.3.2, Equations (14)–(20); page 14, Algorithm 1; pages 42–44, Appendix D, especially Equations (D-2) and (D-9). The online model inherits the move in Equation (28), page 17. Appendix E, pages 44–45, confirms that the common-eigenvector variant is used in the experiments. All page numbers refer to the original PDF.

**Claim.** The paper's principal methodological contribution extends reversible-jump MCMC to von Mises–Fisher mixtures. It defines an invertible split transformation and deterministic inverse merge, using their change-of-variables Jacobian in the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance ratio. Equation (17) first applies Gaussian-style Euclidean shifts to the parent mean and then normalizes both child means to unit length, as required by the vMF model. Equations (18)–(19) and Appendix D are presented as the inverse and Jacobian of that transformation. This kernel is used for posterior inference over the number of components in both TvMFMM and OTvMFMM.

**Error and evidence.** Normalizing the two children destroys the stated inverse. The following example satisfies the paper's sampling supports, positive covariance and adjacency requirements, including the common-eigenvector setting actually used in the main experiments.

Take dimension \(D=2\), one nonempty parent of weight \(1\), and parent mean direction \(\mu_*=(0,1)^T\). Use four unit observations: two copies each of

\[
x_-=(-4/5,3/5)^T,\qquad x_+=(4/5,3/5)^T.
\]

The paper's own Equation (3) gives the positive-definite empirical scatter

\[
\Sigma_*={1\over3}\sum_{i=1}^4(x_i-\mu_*)(x_i-\mu_*)^T
=\operatorname{diag}(64/75,16/75).
\]

Its ascending eigenvalues are \(\lambda_*=(16/75,64/75)\), with eigenvector matrix \(V_*=[e_2,e_1]\). Keep these eigenvectors common to both children, as the paper permits. Select the auxiliary variables

\[
u_1=1/2,\qquad u_2=(3\sqrt3/8,\sqrt3/8)^T,
\qquad u_3=(1/2,1/2)^T.
\]

All are strictly inside their respective Beta and Uniform supports in Equation (16). The shift in Equation (17) is exactly

\[
\sum_d u_{2d}\sqrt{\lambda_{*d}}V_{*d}=(1/5,3/10)^T.
\]

The proposed weights are \(\pi_1=\pi_2=1/2\); both children have positive eigenvalues \((37/300,61/75)\). Their normalized mean directions are

\[
\mu_1={(-2,7)^T\over\sqrt{53}},\qquad
\mu_2={(2,13)^T\over\sqrt{173}}.
\]

They satisfy \(\mu_1<\mu_2\) even componentwise, and no third component can lie between them. Thus the adjacency check does not remove this example. Assign the two \(x_-\) observations to child 1 and the two \(x_+\) observations to child 2. Both children are nonempty and this allocation has positive probability for any finite positive vMF concentrations and positive mixing weights.

Equation (18) now merges these children to

\[
\widetilde\mu_*
={\mu_1+\mu_2\over\|\mu_1+\mu_2\|}
\approx(-0.06278384496,\;0.99802714833)^T,
\]

which is not the original \((0,1)^T\). Its first coordinate is strictly negative because \(-2/\sqrt{53}+2/\sqrt{173}<0\). Before normalizing the children, their weighted mean is exactly the original parent; the failure arises at the normalization step. The strict support, adjacency and non-inverse inequalities persist in a neighborhood, so this is not an isolated zero-probability proposal.

The acceptance correction does not account for this loss of invertibility. At the same example, Equation (D-9) gives

\[
|\det J|={1155584\over421875}>0.
\]

Independent symbolic differentiation confirms that this is the determinant of the **unnormalized Euclidean** split. For a normalized vector \(n(v)=v/\|v\|\), the derivative is

\[
Dn(v)={I-n(v)n(v)^T\over\|v\|}.
\]

The blocks in (D-2), such as \(\partial\mu_1/\partial\mu_*=I\), omit these factors. Including normalization gives two unit-output constraints, hence a singular ambient derivative rather than the nonzero determinant used by the paper.

This cannot be fixed by interpreting that zero determinant as a valid manifold Jacobian. Even granting the paper's expanded eigenvalue state and common eigenvectors, a unit parent plus the \(2D+1\) auxiliaries has dimension \(4D+1\), while the two unit children, their weights and eigenvalues have dimension \(4D\). The stated deterministic map is not a dimension-matched bijection on the appropriate spaces. It needs a different proposal construction, fewer forward auxiliaries or additional reverse auxiliaries with their densities, and a new acceptance law.

In particular, the claimed reverse move does not return the forward parent. The target density, auxiliary density, allocation probability and printed determinant are finite and positive at ordinary positive prior/concentration settings; the specified acceptance formula has no factor correcting the missing reverse proposal. Therefore the derivation does not define the claimed reversible posterior-sampling kernel. This conclusion concerns the algorithm as written; it does not claim that every possible nonreversible kernel must fail to have a stationary distribution.

**Reason for rejection.** The new split–merge extension is a central contribution, used to justify posterior component counts and model exploration in both proposed models. Its asserted inverse and change-of-variables calculation fail under the paper's own conditions. Consequently the posterior interpretation of the reported trans-dimensional inference is unsupported. Repair requires redesigning this move and its acceptance probability, then rerunning the inference and comparisons that use it. Dropping normalization violates the model's unit-mean requirement. Deleting the split–merge move and using a different birth–death-only sampler could be an alternative method, but removes the advertised extension and does not validate the reported chain. These are substantive changes to the central method, warranting rejection of the paper as written.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the vMF split–merge derivation, I noticed that Gaussian moment-preserving shifts were followed by unit normalization, while the reverse equations and appendix derivatives retained the unnormalized Gaussian formulas.

**Verification method.** I read all 51 pages, including Appendices A–I, and rechecked the rendered move definitions, reverse equations and appendix Jacobian. Exact arithmetic verified the unit-vector data, empirical covariance, ordered eigenvalues, proposal supports, child parameters, adjacency and failed round trip. Symbolic differentiation verified the nonzero unnormalized determinant and two exact left-null vectors after normalization. One hundred further numerical cases recovered the parent before normalization and failed after normalization. An independent auditor reread the relevant original pages and checked the same construction and dimension mismatch.

 Twenty separate fixed-component conjugacy checks against circle integration passed, so this finding does not indiscriminately reject the valid fixed-component formulas. The original Python sampler, Wikipedia feature matrices, raw MCMC chains and experimental seeds were not recovered. I do not assert that the published ARI, coherence or churn numbers are fabricated or numerically false, and this is not an author-code rerun. The inverse, dimension and Jacobian defects are one underlying error in the Gaussian-to-spherical move construction.

**Confidence.** High. The exact counterexample satisfies all stated restrictions relevant to the move, including the experimental common-eigenvector variant. The symbolic derivative and intrinsic dimension count independently confirm that the printed change-of-variables argument does not apply.

which is not the original \((0,1)^T\). Its first coordinate is strictly negative because \(-2/\sqrt{53}+2/\sqrt{173}<0\). Before normalizing the children, their weighted mean is exactly the original parent; the failure arises at the normalization step. The strict support, adjacency and non-inverse inequalities persist in a neighborhood, so this is not an isolated zero-probability proposal.

The acceptance correction does not account for this loss of invertibility. At the same example, Equation (D-9) gives

\[ |\det J|={1155584\over421875}>0. \]

Independent symbolic differentiation confirms that this is the determinant of the unnormalized Euclidean split. For a normalized vector \(n(v)=v/\|v\|\), the derivative is

\[ Dn(v)={I-n(v)n(v)^T\over\|v\|}. \]

The blocks in (D-2), such as \(\partial\mu_1/\partial\mu_*=I\), omit these factors. Including normalization gives two unit-output constraints, hence a singular ambient derivative rather than the nonzero determinant used by the paper.

This cannot be fixed by interpreting that zero determinant as a valid manifold Jacobian. Even granting the paper's expanded eigenvalue state and common eigenvectors, a unit parent plus the \(2D+1\) auxiliaries has dimension \(4D+1\), while the two unit children, their weights and eigenvalues have dimension \(4D\). The stated deterministic map is not a dimension-matched bijection on the appropriate spaces. It needs a different proposal construction, fewer forward auxiliaries or additional reverse auxiliaries with their densities, and a new acceptance law.

In particular, the claimed reverse move does not return the forward parent. The target density, auxiliary density, allocation probability and printed determinant are finite and positive at ordinary positive prior/concentration settings; the specified acceptance formula has no factor correcting the missing reverse proposal. Therefore the derivation does not define the claimed reversible posterior-sampling kernel. This conclusion concerns the algorithm as written; it does not claim that every possible nonreversible kernel must fail to have a stationary distribution.

Reason for rejection. The new split–merge extension is a central contribution, used to justify posterior component counts and model exploration in both proposed models. Its asserted inverse and change-of-variables calculation fail under the paper's own conditions. Consequently the posterior interpretation of the reported trans-dimensional inference is unsupported. Repair requires redesigning this move and its acceptance probability, then rerunning the inference and comparisons that use it. Dropping normalization violates the model's unit-mean requirement. Deleting the split–merge move and using a different birth–death-only sampler could be an alternative method, but removes the advertised extension and does not validate the reported chain. These are substantive changes to the central method, warranting rejection of the paper as written.

Discovery method. While tracing the vMF split–merge derivation, I noticed that Gaussian moment-preserving shifts were followed by unit normalization, while the reverse equations and appendix derivatives retained the unnormalized Gaussian formulas.

Verification method. I read all 51 pages, including Appendices A–I, and rechecked the rendered move definitions, reverse equations and appendix Jacobian. Exact arithmetic verified the unit-vector data, empirical covariance, ordered eigenvalues, proposal supports, child parameters, adjacency and failed round trip. Symbolic differentiation verified the nonzero unnormalized determinant and two exact left-null vectors after normalization. One hundred further numerical cases recovered the parent before normalization and failed after normalization. An independent auditor reread the relevant original pages and checked the same construction and dimension mismatch.

Twenty separate fixed-component conjugacy checks against circle integration passed, so this finding does not indiscriminately reject the valid fixed-component formulas. The original Python sampler, Wikipedia feature matrices, raw MCMC chains and experimental seeds were not recovered. I do not assert that the published ARI, coherence or churn numbers are fabricated or numerically false, and this is not an author-code rerun. The inverse, dimension and Jacobian defects are one underlying error in the Gaussian-to-spherical move construction.

findings.title: The proposed hard-partition KL criterion degenerates to graph connected components
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-549__I01 — The proposed hard-partition KL criterion degenerates to graph connected components
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pp. 2–4, the KL choice and NOSAC definition; p. 6, Eq. (8); p. 9, the post-discretization selection procedure and Section 3.5; p. 11, Section 4.2; p. 15, the claimed closeness of the soft and discrete residuals. The cluster-count contribution is highlighted in the abstract and the new-contribution list on p. 3.

**Claim.** The paper defines a hard partition by an indicator matrix \(\bar F\), and normalizes it to

\[
M_{ij}=\begin{cases}1/|C_k|,&i,j\in C_k,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
\]

It chooses forward generalized KL divergence as its discrepancy:

\[
D_{\rm KL}(S\|M)=\sum_{ij}\left[S_{ij}\log\frac{S_{ij}}{M_{ij}}-S_{ij}+M_{ij}\right].
\]

The proposed cluster-count procedure runs DCD for candidate counts, discretizes its output into a hard partition, and selects the smallest resulting NOSAC residual. The introduction also proposes minimizing this criterion over all hard partitions to determine the number of clusters. The declared experimental similarities are symmetrized, binarized 10-nearest-neighbor graphs.

**Error and evidence.** If \(S_{ij}>0\) crosses a hard partition, \(M_{ij}=0\) and that term is \(+\infty\). The convention \(0\log0=0\) does not remove a positive numerator over zero. Consequently, the hard score is finite **if and only if every positive-affinity connected component is entirely contained within one cluster**. On a connected graph, all nontrivial hard partitions have infinite score, whereas the single-cluster partition has finite score.

An exact input follows the paper's actual graph construction. Take twelve one-dimensional data points

\[
x_i=i,\qquad i=0,\ldots,11.
\]

Connect each point to its ten nearest other points, symmetrize, and binarize. The resulting graph is complete except for the edge between 0 and 11, with zero diagonal and 130 directed positive entries. It is connected. Hence every partition into two or more nonempty clusters scores \(+\infty\), independently of how DCD found the partition. For one cluster, \(M_{ij}=1/12\), giving

\[
D_{\rm KL}(S\|M)=130\log12-118\approx205.03786447244<\infty.
\]

Independent enumeration of all 2,047 distinct nontrivial binary partitions found at least 20 directed positive cross-edges in every case. Connectedness proves the same result for every count greater than one, beyond the enumerated binary case. Positive rescaling of the affinities does not change this obstruction.

The degeneracy is also explicit for disconnected graphs. Let a positive-edge connected component have size \(n_c\) and affinity mass \(a_c>0\). In a finite-scoring partition, the partition-dependent part of the score is

\[
\sum_c a_c\log |C(c)|,
\]

where \(C(c)\) is the cluster containing that component. Merging components strictly increases this expression. Thus, when every component has positive affinity mass, the global minimum simply returns the connected components. This is a restriction of the criterion's finite domain, rather than a clustering algorithm occasionally failing to match arbitrary ground-truth labels.

The soft approximation does not resolve the hard-score definition. Positive soft assignments give a finite score, while their hard discretization can have infinite score, contrary to the stated soft/discrete closeness. Substituting the soft score would also require a different model-selection argument: splitting a column \(w\) into \(tw\) and \((1-t)w\) preserves both row sums and \(B=\sum_k w_kw_k^T/(\mathbf1^Tw_k)\). The soft feasible spaces are nested, so the globally minimized soft discrepancy cannot increase with the allowed count.

**Reason for rejection.** Automatic selection of the number of clusters is an explicit central contribution and a stated advance over the earlier 2012 method. Its written hard-partition criterion cannot compare any nontrivial candidates on connected graphs admitted by the paper's own input procedure; if one cluster is allowed it always wins. This invalidates the method as specified for that central contribution. A finite affinity floor or a smoothed incidence matrix would define a different criterion: cross-edge mass acquires a term proportional to \(\log(1/\epsilon)\), introducing a smoothing choice whose effect must be described and validated. Changing to a different divergence or to a soft score also changes the proposed selection rule. The paper supplies no such definition or justification. This cannot be resolved by correcting an isolated arithmetic constant while retaining the stated criterion.

The matrix-decomposition equivalence and fixed-count clustering method are not refuted. Nor does this report assert that the exact historical Table 3/Figure 2 inputs were connected, or that the reported finite curves could not have arisen from some different, undocumented implementation. Their original 2016 scoring driver and the cited final supplement remain unavailable.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the passage from positive soft assignments to hard cluster-count evaluation, I noticed that hard incidence matrices introduce zeros at cross-cluster pairs, exactly where forward KL is singular.

**Verification method.** I reread the full paper and appendices, inspected the original rendered definitions, KL objective, selection procedure and experimental description, proved the finite-domain characterization, and enumerated the exact 12-point 10NN input. A separate reviewer independently checked the bounded original passages and reconstructed the cut/connected-component certificate. I also inspected the author's released 2012 MATLAB code and executed its unchanged DCD routine and C helpers under Octave: that code returns a **soft** score and contains no 2016 hard-partition cluster-count driver. It does not establish how the historical Table 3 curves were produced.

 Detailed source and coverage limits are in that paper's `hard-KL-candidate.md`, `source-retrieval.json` and `supplement-retries.json`.

**Confidence: High.** The failure follows directly from the paper's hard matrix and forward-KL definitions, and the example satisfies its explicit similarity construction. Exact enumeration and independent bounded review confirm the argument. Confidence does not extend to an attribution of a specific historical implementation or score error; those artifacts were not recovered.

findings.title: The separation premise is unattainable for every nontrivial asymptotic clustering model
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-553__I01 — The separation premise is unattainable for every nontrivial asymptotic clustering model
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF p. 12, Eq. (7) and the pairwise grouping penalty; pp. 13–14, the parameter space, \(\mathcal B\), \(C_{\min}\), and Assumption (A2); p. 15, Theorem 2 and its claimed applications; pp. 16–17, Proposition 1 and the proposed shrinking-separation/many-cluster regimes. Supporting derivations are in Appendix A, pp. 20–23.

**Claim.** The paper presents a new general clustering-consistency theory for the global \(L_0\)-constrained estimator. It claims that its conditions permit multiple clusters, increasing dimension, a growing number of clusters, and decreasing distances between true centroids. Its estimator constrains

\[
J(\mu)=\sum_{i<j}\mathbf1\{\mu_i\ne\mu_j\}\le J(\mu^*).
\]

The paper defines

\[
\mathcal B=\{\mu:C(\mu)\ne C(\mu^*),\ J(\mu)\le J(\mu^*)\},\qquad
C_{\min}(\mu^*)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal B}
\frac{h_a^2(f_\mu,f_{\mu^*})}{|C(\mu)|}.
\]

Assumption (A2) requires a fixed \(d_1>0\) such that

\[
C_{\min}(\mu^*)>\frac{d_1m\log n}{n},
\]

where the minimal disjoint centering number \(m\) is a positive integer. The candidate space in Eq. (7), \(C\), and \(\mathcal B\) is defined over unrestricted centroid vectors; no geometric or minimum-intersection filter is included in those definitions.

**Error and evidence.** For every true partition with \(K\ge2\) nonempty clusters,

\[
C_{\min}(\mu^*)\le\frac{1}{n(K-1)}\le\frac1n.
\]

The proof is elementary and independent of the distribution, dimension, or centroid separation:

1. Choose one observation from a smallest true cluster of size \(a\), and change only its centroid to the centroid of a different largest cluster of size \(b\ge a\).
2. For cluster sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_K\), \(J=(n^2-\sum_k n_k^2)/2\). This move changes the penalty by
   \[
   J_{\rm new}-J_{\rm true}=a-b-1<0.
   \]
   Thus the changed vector belongs to the paper's \(\mathcal B\).
3. Only one per-observation density changes. The normalized Hellinger distance used in the paper satisfies \(h\le1\), so \(h_a^2\le1/n\). This follows both from the printed \(h_a=\sum_i h_i/\sqrt n\) and from the conventional root-mean-square averaged Hellinger metric, if that notation is corrected.
4. If \(a>1\), the candidate retains \(K\) clusters; if \(a=1\), it has \(K-1\). In either case its cluster count is at least \(K-1\), proving the bound.

But (A2) then implies

\[
\frac{1}{K-1}>d_1m\log n,
\]

which is impossible eventually for any \(K\ge2\), fixed \(d_1>0\), and \(m\ge1\). Growing separation cannot remove the obstruction because normalized Hellinger distance is bounded by one. The argument also applies to perfectly disjoint distributions; it is not an objection based on Gaussian overlap at a fixed separation.

The claimed truncated-Gaussian application fails explicitly as well. Proposition 1 defines

\[
r_{\alpha_{\min}}=
\frac{\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal B}\inf_{\alpha_{\min}-\|\mu_i-\mu_i^*\|^2\le t\le\alpha_{\min}}
\chi_p(t/4)}{4\,\mathsf X_p(\alpha_{\min}/4)},
\]

where \(\chi_p\) is the chi-square density and \(\mathsf X_p\) its distribution function. Choose a closest pair of true centroids, and move one observation from the smaller of those two groups to the larger. The same penalty calculation makes the move admissible, and \(\|\mu_i-\mu_i^*\|^2=\alpha_{\min}\). The inner interval therefore includes \(t=0\). For \(p\ge3\), \(\chi_p(0)=0\), while the denominator is positive. Consequently,

\[
r_{\alpha_{\min}}=0,
\]

so the proposed positive sufficient condition cannot hold. Excluding the endpoint alone would not help: the infimum as \(t\downarrow0\) remains zero. This contradicts the subsequent positive/diverging interpretation used to claim the new consistency regimes. In addition, (A3) quantifies over all centroid vectors; singleton candidate intersections force its uniform \(m_1\le1\), excluding the proposed \(m_1=n^{h_1}\), \(h_1>0\), example.

These results show that the stated theory has **no nontrivial asymptotic application** in its defined parameter space. They do not furnish a counterexample satisfying (A2), and this report does not call the conditional statement of Theorem 2 false. Its asymptotic premise is unattainable, so it cannot supply the advertised guarantee.

**Reason for rejection.** A new general consistency theory is a principal contribution in the title, abstract and introduction. Under its own definitions, that contribution gives no asymptotic guarantee for any clustering with two or more groups, including the concrete family offered to establish applicability. Removing the unsupported theoretical applications would remove a central new contribution. Repair requires a different separation notion and likelihood/complexity analysis, or a changed restricted estimator and parameter class. Silently excluding one-observation alternatives would change Eq. (7) and \(\mathcal B\); changing a numerical constant, reversing the entropy logarithm, or correcting the averaged-metric notation cannot fix the bound above. The empirical DC-ADMM method and its reported speed comparisons are not refuted by this finding.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the consistency proof, I noticed that its pair-count constraint was treated as a bound on the number of clusters. Examining the feasible alternative partitions then exposed the one-observation upper bound on the separation quantity.

**Verification method.** I read the entire paper and appendices and rechecked the original rendered definitions, theorem, truncated example and proofs. Exact integer checks verified the penalty change across thousands of cluster-size configurations; the universal Hellinger bound proves the asymptotic obstruction. A separate reviewer independently read the bounded original passages and verified the same argument, the chi-square endpoint, and the singleton-intersection condition. The authentic July 2016 CRAN release was inspected and compiled unchanged; targeted native optimizer tests agreed with exact convex special cases. Those software checks are separate from the theory certificate and are not historical experiment reruns.

**Confidence: High.** The obstruction uses the exact unrestricted alternative set, exact pair-count algebra, and the normalized Hellinger bound. It persists under routine notation corrections and is independent of distributional tails or numerical approximations. Independent original-PDF review confirmed the relevant quantifiers and interval endpoints.

findings.title: Negative ball scores make the promoted RW-CCCD classifier undefined on admissible imbalanced inputs
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-604__I01 — Negative ball scores make the promoted RW-CCCD classifier undefined on admissible imbalanced inputs
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 10, Equations (3)–(5); page 11, Algorithm 3, lines 6 and 8; page 12, unnumbered RW-CCCD classification rule; page 15, pilot tuning grid. Central contribution: pages 1–3 and 32–35.

**Claim.** For a target sample of size n and non-target sample of size m, the random walk is

R_x(r) = (m/n) · #{target points within r} − #{non-target points within r}.

Algorithm 3 maximizes this walk to choose r_x, then selects the ball with largest

T_x = R_x(r_x) − r_x n_u / (2 d_m(x)),

where n_u is the number of remaining target points and d_m(x) is the largest original target distance from x. The classification rule minimizes, over the class covers and their balls,

rho(z,x)^(T_x^e), where rho(z,x)=d(z,x)/r_x and e∈[0,1].

Page 15 explicitly tunes e over 0,.1,…,1. The exponent is the nested power T_x^e. There is no positive-score assumption, absolute value, positive part or other score transformation in the stated rule.

**Error and evidence.** Scores can be strictly negative on ordinary well-separated imbalanced training sets. An exact witness satisfying the paper's Figure 9 dimensions, supports and sample sizes is:

- n=400, m=20, d=2, delta=1;
- X={(1/10+i/2000, 1/10+j/2000): i,j=0,…,19};
- Y={(11/10+i/2000, 11/10+i²/40000): i=0,…,19}.

Every X point is strictly inside (0,1)^2; every Y point is strictly inside (1,2)^2. Both classes contain distinct points. Every within-class distance is smaller than every cross-class distance. For example, the largest squared within-X distance is 361/2000000, whereas the smallest squared cross distance is 3924361/2000000. Thus, for every X center, the random walk strictly increases at target distance values until all 400 target points are included, before encountering any non-target point. Its unique maximizing radius value is r_x=d_m(x)>0. At that radius R_x=20, so

T_x = 20 − 400/2 = −180.

All candidate X centers have this same negative score. Every possible tie choice covers the entire target sample in one iteration, storing a positive-radius ball with score −180. Reversing the roles, every Y center has R_y=400, r_y=d_m(y)>0 and score 400−20/2=390. Both class fits therefore finish in one iteration, with no later normalization or update ambiguity.

At e=1/2, expressly included in the tuning grid, the majority exponent requires sqrt(−180). It is not real, so the published real-valued class minimum is undefined for an ordinary test point at positive distance from the centers. This is not a zero-radius, singleton, duplicate-point or tie-breaking defect. Every coordinate is in the strict interior of its prescribed support, and all distance inequalities are strict, so an open neighborhood of the witness has the same failure. It consequently has positive probability under the specified independent continuous uniform sampling protocol.

A smaller check uses six target points {(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(0,1),(1,1),(2,1)} and two non-target points {(100,100),(101,101)}. The same cancellation gives every majority score −1 and every minority score 5, making the failure directly checkable by hand. Native R arithmetic returns NaN for (−1)^.5. More generally, whenever all cross distances exceed all within distances, the majority score is m−n/2, which is negative for n>2m.

Independent first-step controls on fresh samples from the disclosed n400/m20 shifted-unit-cube experiment also select a negative score in all 40 delta1 repetitions (ten each at d2/3/5/10), and in many overlapping cases, including 8/10 at d10/delta.5. These checks corroborate that the mechanism is not confined to the small constructed cluster; they are not a proof that every uniform sample fails, or a reproduction/refutation of a reported historical AUC.

The paper's main result is empirical robustness and compact classification using this method; P-CCCD is an existing alternative and is often weaker in the paper's strong-baseline comparisons. A reader cannot execute the stated RW tuning procedure on the witness.

Repair requires specifying a different positive-score transformation, changing the radius/penalty normalization or optimization, or withdrawing the fractional tuning family. These alter selected covers and/or relative ball and class powers, rather than giving an algebraically equivalent value for the published rule. For example, moving the penalty inside the radius maximization changes the radii and may select ignored zero-radius balls; rescaling the penalty changes the competition between centers; clipping or replacing negative scores changes the decision boundary. No verified implementation establishes that the published formula is merely a transcription of an already validated equivalent classifier. This warrants rejection of the paper as written, pending that substantive definition and revalidation.

A recovered historical implementation demonstrating a local transcription error and preserving the actual validated classifier could change the disposition. No such artifact was found.

Verified exact integer-coordinate distance/count controls for the strict-interior n400/m20 witness and exact Fraction controls for the smaller example; no relevant assumption is violated. An independent bounded reviewer checked the original pages and separately recomputed the strict-interior certificate. Saved fresh-sample first-step controls with seeds and data.

The author's later PCDSL repository has no RW implementation. The author's 2017 dissertation repeats the disputed formulas without resolving positivity. The cited DeVinney2002 proceedings were recovered from a2005 Wayback capture and all ten pages read, with its original pages4/6 rendered: it gives normalized R, radius argmax(R−P), a separate score R(r*)−p(r*), and an unspecified cover-distance choice; it does not give a positive fractional-score convention for the 2016 rule. findings.title: The practical safe threshold does not have the advertised exact-support guarantee
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-605__I01 — The practical safe threshold does not have the advertised exact-support guarantee
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 5, Remark 4 following Theorem 3; pages 11–12, Figures 3 and 4 captions; page 13, variable-selection simulation procedure and riboflavin application; page 14, Table 1 and conclusion. The definitions are on pages 3–4 and the main proof is on page 15.

**Claim.** Under Assumption 1, with Cbar ≥ C, let lambda_star be the smallest grid value for which P(||X'epsilon||infinity/n ≤ lambda/4) ≥ 1−delta. Remark 4 asserts exact support recovery after thresholding beta_hat(lambda_hat) by 3 Cbar lambda_hat whenever beta_min > 6 Cbar lambda_star. Theorem 3 itself bounds error by 3 Cbar lambda_star and gives lambda_hat ≤ lambda_star. Page 13 expressly applies the lambda_hat threshold in Figures 3/4 and Table 1, motivating the unthresholded CV comparison by calling the AV threshold theoretically safe.

**Error and evidence.** Take n=4, p=2 and X with rows

(1,1), (1,−1), (−1,1), (−1,−1).

Its columns are centered and normalized, and X'X/n=I. Set beta_star=(100,0). Let epsilon=Z Xcol2, where Z is equally likely to be −1 or +1. Every noise coordinate has mean zero and variance one; noise dependence is expressly allowed by the paper. Then Y=X(100,Z), the OLS statistic is (100,Z), and the unique Lasso solution under the published squared-loss/n normalization is

beta_hat(lambda) = soft((100,Z), lambda/2).

The noise score is X'epsilon/n=(0,Z), so T_lambda occurs exactly when lambda ≥ 4. On the finite increasing grid

Lambda = {1/100, 4, 200},

the oracle lambda_star=4 for every delta∈(0,1). Moreover, lambda_max=2||X'Y||infinity/n=200 deterministically, exactly as required. Assumption 1 holds with C=3/4: on T_lambda the coordinatewise soft-threshold error is at most lambda/4 + lambda/2 = 3 lambda/4. At the grid points, T is empty at 1/100; at 4 and 200 the errors are 2 and 100. Both the recommended Cbar=3/4 and the larger Cbar=5/4 satisfy Cbar ≥ C.

Soft thresholding is 1-Lipschitz in its threshold, so for every pair lambda,mu,

||beta_hat(lambda)−beta_hat(mu)||infinity ≤ |lambda−mu|/2.

Every AV test therefore has its normalized difference at most 1/2 < Cbar. The exact definition and Algorithm 1 select lambda_hat=1/100 for both possible noise outcomes. The estimate is

(19999/200, Z·199/200) = (99.995, ±.995).

For Cbar=3/4, the claimed safe threshold is 9/400=.0225 and the beta-min condition is 100>18. The inactive second coefficient has magnitude 199/200, so it survives: the estimated support is {1,2}, whereas the true support is {1}. For Cbar=5/4, the threshold is 3/80=.0375 and the beta-min condition is 100>30; it also fails. Exact support recovery thus fails with probability one despite every stated condition, a finite oracle, a correct grid endpoint and a perfectly conditioned design.

The invalid inference compares the oracle-scale error bound with a smaller selected-scale threshold. The inequality lambda_hat ≤ lambda_star has the wrong direction for eliminating false positives at 3 Cbar lambda_hat. Thresholding at 3 Cbar lambda_star would be justified, but that oracle is unknown.

**Reason for rejection.** Finite-sample variable selection is explicitly a main theoretical contribution on page 2 and a goal reiterated on page 14. The invalid safe threshold is also the procedure used for the support-selection comparison and biological gene list. This is a false principal guarantee and an invalid theoretical safety justification for the implemented selection rule, rather than an unattached supporting remark.

Replacing lambda_hat by unknown lambda_star abandons the practical, noise-adaptive threshold. No finite multiplier repairs the current procedure: for any finite K, choose lambda_min < 1/(K Cbar + 1/2). AV still accepts every test, while the inactive magnitude 1−lambda_min/2 exceeds K Cbar lambda_min. Increasing the beta-min requirement cannot eliminate this noise-only false positive; the active signal can be made arbitrarily large. Restoring the guarantee requires a different noise-calibrated threshold/procedure or a substantive condition tying the lower grid endpoint to unknown noise. That changes or withdraws the principal practical support-recovery contribution and warrants rejection of the paper as written.

The main Theorem 3 sup-norm estimation bound and inclusion of sufficiently strong active variables survive. No reported historical simulation average or biological coefficient is claimed numerically false. Historical experiments may still favor the method in selected settings.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the conversion of Theorem 3's oracle-scale bound into Remark 4's selected-scale threshold, noticed the reversed comparison. Tested the paper's own best-case orthogonal design, where the entire Lasso path is explicit.

**Verification method.** Read all 20 pages, including Appendices A–C, and rechecked the relevant original rendered definitions, theorem, threshold, experiment and proof pages. Enumerated every grid-pair test and both noise outcomes with exact Fractions, verifying all assumptions and failure probability one. Ran authentic historical glmnet 2.0-2 at its correctly converted lambda/2, using the centered orthogonal X without intercept or standardization; coefficients and failed support agree within 4.2e−15. An independent bounded reviewer inspected original pages 1–8 and 11–17, including full renders 5/13/14, and separately verified both signs and Cbar values with exact arithmetic. Its saved certificate agrees.

Continued the full-paper checks after discovery. Separate numerical controls on 101 arbitrary-design paths with certified sup-norm constants preserve the main estimation guarantee (maximum KKT residual below 7.8e−13). Ran six fresh fixed-seed SNR-5 simulations using historical glmnet across p=300/900 and correlation 0/.4/.9; these are targeted controls, not the historical 100-replicate figures. Recovered the March 2016 hdi riboflavin data. Explicit preprocessing alternatives do not identify the original author driver, so their Table 1 mismatch is a reproduction limit, not another finding. Publisher, MIT mirror, author publications and repository searches did not recover the historical AV experimental driver.

**Confidence.** High. The counterexample uses exact arithmetic, unique Lasso solutions and a permitted mean-zero finite-variance noise distribution; failure occurs for every noise outcome. Original rendered assumptions and an independent exact certificate agree. The arbitrary-multiplier obstruction rules out a missing constant. Severity is confined to the expressly promoted practical support guarantee, with the separate estimation theorem and historical numerical values preserved.

findings.title: The closed-form supervised fit does not maximize its claimed Spearman objective
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-625__I01 — The closed-form supervised fit does not maximize its claimed Spearman objective
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 3, Section 1.1 (claimed contribution); PDF pages 19–20, Sections 6.1–6.2, the conversion to Equation (16), learning step 3, and the paragraph immediately below that step; PDF page 24, Section 7. Appendix A on PDF pages 26–27 states the squared-distance identity used in the conversion.

**Claim.** The paper presents its learned expert weights as maximizing Spearman correlation with a specified target ranking. Section 6 first replaces the ranked weighted product with the unranked product in Equation (16), then minimizes squared differences of logarithmic ranks. PDF page 20 explicitly asserts that the latter change still solves Equation (16) and maximizes Spearman correlation through Equation (1). The experimental version adds an intercept to the logarithmic least-squares fit. Section 6 permits real expert weights; no positivity restriction, minimum number of experts, missing-rank requirement, or special target-order restriction excludes the example below.

**Error and evidence.** Dropping the rank operator and changing the loss to log-space squared error changes the optimization objective. Monotonicity of logarithms preserves the ordering of a fixed score vector; it does not imply that fitting different weights by a different loss preserves, or optimizes, the target rank correlation.

Here is a complete, tie-free counterexample to the version with the experimental intercept. Take four objects, one expert, and normalized complete ranks

\[
R=(1,2,3,4)/5,\qquad L=(3,2,1,4)/5.
\]

Execute the stated least-squares step with an intercept:

\[
(\widehat\beta,\widehat\omega)
=\arg\min_{\beta,\omega}\sum_{i=1}^4
[\log L_i-\beta-\omega\log R_i]^2.
\]

Its design has full column rank. The sign of its unique fitted slope is the sign of the centered logarithmic cross-product. Let \(a=\log 2>0\) and \(b=\log 3\). Normalizing the ranks by five only adds constants, which disappear on centering. The cross-product is exactly

\[
S_{\log R,\log L}
=5a^2-\frac{(3a+b)^2}{4}
=\frac{11a^2-6ab-b^2}{4}<0.
\]

Indeed, \(3^2>2^3\) gives \(b/a>3/2\), so
\(11-6(b/a)-(b/a)^2<11-9-9/4=-1/4\).
Thus \(\widehat\omega<0\) exactly. Numerically the fit is
\(\widehat\beta\simeq-0.9071808026\),
\(\widehat\omega\simeq-0.1132084664\).
The weighted geometric scores \(e^{\widehat\beta}R_i^{\widehat\omega}\) consequently have ranks \((4,3,2,1)\).

Using the paper’s Equation (1), their Spearman correlation with target ranks \((3,2,1,4)\) is

\[
1-\frac{6(1+1+1+9)}{4(4^2-1)}=-\frac15.
\]

The admissible alternative \(\omega=1\), with any intercept, instead has ranks \((1,2,3,4)\) and correlation

\[
1-\frac{6(4+0+4+0)}{4(4^2-1)}=+\frac15.
\]

The fitted result is strictly worse by \(2/5\). Since a one-expert power score is increasing, decreasing, or constant, the positive-weight ordering is also the best nonconstant ordering available to this model. If the paper’s finite plug-in Equation (9) is used for the two ranked variables instead, the corresponding values are \(-3/25\) and \(+3/25\), respectively, so that convention does not resolve the failure.

The intercept-free algorithm as printed also fails: for two objects, \(R=(1,2)/3\) and \(L=(2,1)/3\), the fitted coefficient is
\(\widehat\omega=\langle\log R,\log L\rangle/\|\log R\|^2>0\), because both log vectors have strictly negative entries. It produces correlation \(-1\), whereas the permitted weight \(-1\) produces \(+1\). The four-object construction above shows that adding the experimental intercept does not repair the problem.

**Reason for rejection.** The affected contribution is the claimed closed-form solution of supervised Spearman-optimal weighting, explicitly identified in Section 1.1 and used to derive RAGS in Section 6. The counterexample is a failure of the stated algorithm on admissible complete rankings, rather than a missing proof or an imputation edge case. Theorem 17 correctly orders a fixed set of expert lists; it does not validate the subsequent optimization over weights after changing the objective. Keeping the algorithm and calling it a log-rank regression surrogate withdraws this principal optimization claim and its theoretical justification for the learned weights. Restoring the promised objective requires retaining the induced ranking or otherwise solving a different weight-selection problem; adjusting a normalization, coefficient, intercept, or local proof step does not make the published least-squares solution a Spearman optimizer. This warrants rejection of the paper as written. This finding does not refute Theorem 17 or demonstrate that the published benchmark numbers are false.

findings.title: The central coefficient bound fails for an admitted fixed continuous feature distribution
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2016__accepted__v17-15-654__I01 — The central coefficient bound fails for an admitted fixed continuous feature distribution
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 4 and near-oracle consequence, PDF page 8, Section 3.4; assumptions (A1)–(A6), pages 5–7; proof pages 16–20, particularly Eq. (20) on page 19 and conclusion on page 20. The dependent initializer assertion is Theorem 5, page 10. The abstract, introduction (pages 1–3) and conclusion (14–15) identify these as central contributions.

**Claim.** Under (A1)–(A6) and the tuning parameter in Eq. (8), the L1-SVM coefficient estimator obeys Theorem 4's displayed bound with probability at least `1-2p^(-2q(C1^2-1))`, implying L2 error `O_p(sqrt(q log(p)/n))`. Theorem 5 also claims the probability that any coordinate error exceeds the same lambda tends to zero, providing the required initializer for the two-step oracle construction.

**Error and evidence.** The assumptions bound curvature at the population target without controlling an informative neighborhood uniformly as dimension grows. The following example satisfies all six conditions with uniform constants, yet every empirical minimizer is inconsistent with probability tending to one. It uses nested finite-dimensional marginals of ONE fixed infinite distribution; it does not change a low-dimensional distribution with sample size. All quantities and the finite contradiction are explicit.

### 1. A fixed continuous feature process

Let U,V_0,V_2,V_3,... be independent with density w(u)=3(4-u^2)/32 on [-2,2] and zero elsewhere. Let a=5/12 and P(Y=1|U)=(1+aU)/2. This probability lies in [1/12,11/12]; P(Y=+1)=P(Y=-1)=1/2.

For each fixed coordinate j>=2, set delta_j=j^-4 and eta_j=j^-8. Define s(t)=1 for t<=1, s(t)=1-3(t-1)^2+2(t-1)^3 for 1<t<2, and s(t)=0 for t>=2. Set sigma_j(u)=eta_j+(1-eta_j)s(||u|-1|/delta_j). Thus sigma_j is positive and continuously differentiable, is 1 in the radius-delta_j bands around u=+/-1, and is eta_j outside the radius-2delta_j bands.

Set X_0=1, X_1=U, and X_j=2U+sigma_j(U)(V_0+V_j/2), j>=2. At sample size n observe the first p_n=n^2 features. Observations are iid samples from this fixed process.

For a finite p, write u=x_1 and z_j=(x_j-2u)/sigma_j(u). The class-conditional densities are

 f_p(x)=w(u)(1+a*u) integral_{-2}^2 w(v_0) product_{j=2}^p [(2/sigma_j(u)) w(2(z_j-v_0))] dv_0,
 g_p(x)=w(u)(1-a*u) integral_{-2}^2 w(v_0) product_{j=2}^p [(2/sigma_j(u)) w(2(z_j-v_0))] dv_0.

These are continuous full-dimensional densities on R^p. For fixed p every sigma_j is bounded below by positive eta_j; continuity follows from dominated convergence of a finite product of continuous compactly supported factors. Both have the same compact support and are positive on its interior. The shared V_0 creates correlation; the independent V_j/2 terms ensure full-dimensionality. This does not use a discrete design or a singular density. A1 imposes no uniform bound on density heights or on derivatives as p grows.

### 2. Unique population hinge minimizer

Take beta*=(0,1,0,...,0), with q=1 and active support {1}. Exact integrals:
 integral_{-2}^1 u*w(u)du=-27/128,
 integral_{-2}^1 u^2*w(u)du=81/160,
 E[U^2]=4/5,
 -27/128+(5/12)(81/160)=0.
Thus the active-coordinate population hinge gradient vanishes. Symmetry makes the intercept gradient vanish. Since E[X_j|U,Y]=2U for j>=2, all inactive-coordinate gradients also vanish. The hinge risk is convex and differentiable at beta*, hence beta* is globally minimizing.

At U=+/-1, all sigma_j are 1, regardless of j. Let h=(h_0,h_1,...,h_p), s_h=sum_{j=2}^p h_j. From Eq. (7),
 h'H(beta*)h=(51/128)[h_0^2+(h_1+2s_h)^2+(4/5)s_h^2+(1/5)sum_{j=2}^p h_j^2].
The coefficient 51/128 equals w(1)(1+5/12), with the two balanced margin contributions combined. Cross terms with the intercept cancel by symmetry. The identity
 (h_1+2s_h)^2+(4/5)s_h^2=h_1^2/6+(24/5)(s_h+5h_1/12)^2
therefore gives H(beta*) >= (17/256) I, uniformly over p. For each finite p the Hessian is continuous around beta*; consequently strict local convexity and convexity imply that the global minimizer is UNIQUE. A second minimizer would force a flat segment through the strict-convexity neighborhood.

### 3. Every printed assumption, with uniform constants

A1 (PDF 5): f_p,g_p are the continuous common-support densities above; all moments exist and |X_j|<=4+2+1=7 uniformly. Set M=7.
A2 (PDF 6): q=1, c1=0.
A3 (PDF 7): the support limit in Eq. (10) is 2(q+1)=4. For every row and every 4-sparse d, (X_i'd)^2<=4*7^2||d||_2^2=196||d||_2^2. Thus lambda_max<=196 almost surely, for all n,p. Set M1=200.
A4 (PDF 7): the full-space Hessian lower bound 17/256>1/20 implies the required restricted-cone bound with M2=1/20, for every p and every cone parameter.
A5 (PDF 7): beta*_1=1, c2=1, M3=1; 2c1<c2.
A6 (PDF 7): the true score is ALWAYS U. The conditional score densities are f*(u)=w(u)(1+5u/12), g*(u)=w(u)(1-5u/12). On the FIXED neighborhoods [0.9,1.1] and [-1.1,-0.9], respectively, these lie between 1/4 and 1. Neither the neighborhoods nor density bounds vary with p or n.

Choose c=2, A(alpha)=196, alpha=.05. Then 4p^(-A/M^2+1)=4p^-3<=.05 for n>=3, as required with Eq. (8). Its tuning parameter is lambda=56sqrt(log(n)/n). Choose C1=2, C=1+4sqrt(200) as identified in the proof on PDF 19, and Cbar=1/3. All quantities are fixed uniform constants.

### 4. Every empirical minimizer is inconsistent

Use the last observed proxy X_p, p=n^2. Let E_n be the event that every sampled U_i is outside its radius-2delta_p margin bands. Since total band length is at most 8delta_p and w<=3/8,
 P(E_n)>=1-3n*delta_p=1-3/n^7.
On E_n, X_ip=2X_i1+eta_p(V_i0+V_ip/2), where |V_i0+V_ip/2|<=3.

For ANY coefficient vector with beta_1 !=0, zero beta_1 and add beta_1/2 to beta_p. Keep the intercept and every other coefficient unchanged. The empirical hinge loss increases by at most (3/2)eta_p|beta_1|, because the score change is bounded by this quantity and hinge loss is 1-Lipschitz. The L1 penalty decreases by at least lambda|beta_1|/2, by the triangle inequality. Thus whenever lambda>3eta_p, the objective strictly decreases. This holds for all sufficiently large n.

It follows that EVERY L1-SVM minimizer satisfies beta_hat_1=0 on E_n, independently of the behavior of all other coefficients. Hence both ||beta_hat-beta*||_2 and ||beta_hat-beta*||_infty are at least 1 with probability at least 1-3/n^7.

The Theorem 4 bound is a fixed multiple of sqrt(log(n)/n), so tends to zero. Once its radius is <1, the actual probability of its asserted conclusion is <=3/n^7, whereas the claimed probability is >=1-2p^-6=1-2/n^12. Theorem 5's initializer assertion (PDF 10) also fails, since lambda->0 while sup-norm error is >=1 on E_n. No separate claim about actual two-step LLA output is necessary.

### 5. An entirely finite exact certificate

Set n=2^40, p=2^80. Then delta_p=2^-320, eta_p=2^-640. With t=sqrt(2log(p)/n), lambda=28t and the Theorem 4 radius equals (2240sqrt(2)+340C)t. Use log(2)<7/10, sqrt(2)<3/2, C=1+4sqrt(200)<58. Then t<11/2^20 and the radius is <253880/1048576<1/4. Also log(2)>1/2 yields lambda>224/2^20>3eta_p. Actual success probability is <=3/2^280; the printed lower bound is 1-2/2^480. This is an exact inequality certificate, requiring neither a simulated sample nor floating point asymptotics.

**Reason for rejection.** The named main contribution is a near-oracle coefficient guarantee, with the ultra-high-dimensional initializer extension as a dependent contribution. Both fail on an admitted fixed-distribution sequence even though the population target is unique, its full Hessian has a uniform positive lower bound, and the score-density neighborhoods are fixed. The estimator is inconsistent, rather than merely outside a sharp constant or confidence level. A corrected cover argument, a fixed tuning-constant change, or a pointwise fixed-distribution interpretation cannot restore the claim on this example. A NEW uniform local-curvature or quantitative conditional-geometry condition could exclude it and support a narrower theorem, but would withdraw the principal guarantee for currently admitted models. This changes accept to reject for the paper as written. The finding does not dispute all uses of L1-SVM, historical simulation values, or possible strengthened theorems.

**Discovery method.** Tracing the proof exposed a directional covering step treating normalized hinge increments as homogeneous (pages 16–17), reuse of a fixed-base bound at shifted bases (19), and the unlocalized Taylor remainder (20). These raised suspicion but are not the sole evidence. An initial sample-size-dependent witness was strengthened to the fixed infinite feature process above to remove the distributional-interpretation objection. The proof gaps and dependent initializer failure count as one underlying issue.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original rendered assumptions, theorem and proof pages and both appendices. Re-derived the stationary integrals, full Hessian, completed-square lower bound, fixed score-density bounds, deterministic objective improvement, and exact finite probability/radius contradiction.  An independent bounded review of original assumptions and mathematics confirmed these checks and severity; this was not a second whole-paper review. No authentic historical simulation driver or raw outputs were recovered after publisher, mirror and author-source attempts; no historical rerun or empirical reversal is claimed.

**Confidence.** **High.** One fixed infinite distribution satisfies every printed assumption with explicit uniform constants. A deterministic comparison excludes every empirical minimizer, and exact integration, square completion and a finite probability/radius certificate establish the contradiction independently of simulated data. The scope is the coefficient and initializer assertions; actual two-step LLA output is not separately claimed false.
